en: May that Lord, the Master of Serpents, protect you—He whose body is white and stainless, who bestows yoga and is united with yoga; He who, having abandoned His primordial form, manifests in manifold ways for the sake of favoring the world; whose mass of afflictions is utterly destroyed; who possesses many mouths like a serpent of virulent poison yet is a possessor of sublime enjoyments; who is the source of all knowledge; who has serpents as his ornaments; and for whose eternal pleasure the Lord Śiva resides. (1)
Now begins the instruction on yoga. YS 1.1.

The word "now" (*atha*) has the sense of introducing a subject. It should be understood that the treatise on the instruction of yoga (*yogānuśāsana*) is hereby commenced. Yoga is *samādhi* (concentration).

And that is a quality of the mind (*citta*) pertaining to all stages. The stages of the mind are: the distracted (*kṣipta*), the stupefied (*mūḍha*), the scattered (*vikṣipta*), the one-pointed (*ekāgra*), and the restrained (*niruddha*). Among these, concentration existing in a distracted mind—being subordinate to distraction—is not on the side of yoga.

It proceeds. However, that which illuminates the true object when the mind is one-pointed, attenuates the afflictions, loosens the bonds of karma, and brings about the face-to-face encounter with cessation (nirodha), is designated as "yoga with discernment" (*saṃprajñāta-yoga*). We shall explain later that this [yoga] is accompanied by coarse thought (*vitarka*), accompanied by subtle reflection (*vicāra*), accompanied by joy (*ānanda*), and accompanied by the sense of "I-am-ness" (*asmitā*). When all fluctuations (*vṛtti*) have ceased...
That is asamprajñāta-samādhi.
With the desire to state its definition, this aphorism was set forth:
Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind (citta-vṛtti-nirodha). YS 1.2.

Because no sound is perceived [in that state], even *samprajñāta* (cognitive) yoga is so designated. For the mind (*citta*) is composed of the three *guṇas*, owing to its nature of luminosity (*prakhyā*), activity (*pravṛtti*), and stability (*sthiti*).
Indeed, the *sattva* of the mind, whose form is luminosity, when conjoined with *rajas* and *tamas*, becomes fond of sovereignty and sense-objects.

That same [mind], when permeated by *tamas*, becomes associated with unrighteousness (*adharma*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), lack of dispassion (*avairāgya*), and lack of sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*). That very [mind], when the veil of delusion (*moha*) has been destroyed...
Shining forth on all sides, yet pierced by a trace of *rajas*, it becomes endowed with the powers of knowledge of the *dharmas*, dispassion, and sovereignty.

That same [sattva], when freed from the stain of even the slightest trace of *rajas* and established in its own nature, becomes characterized solely by the discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) of the difference between *sattva* and the Puruṣa, and attains the meditation known as the Cloud of Virtue (*dharmamegha*).
Meditators call that the supreme *prasaṃkhyāna*. The power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), however, is unchanging and does not undergo transition.
This discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*)—which has revealed its object, is pure, infinite, and consists of the quality of goodness (*sattva*)—is the opposite of this [worldly state].
Therefore, the mind, becoming detached from that [discernment], suppresses even that discernment. Being in that state, it becomes accompanied by residual impressions (*saṃskāra*).
This is seedless concentration (*nirbīja-samādhi*). Because nothing is cognized therein, it is "non-cognitive" (*asaṃprajñāta*). It is of two kinds.
"Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind.

(YS 1.2) When the mind is in that state, since there is an absence of objects, what is the nature of the *puruṣa*, whose essence is the awareness of the intellect?—At that time, the seer abides in its own true form. (YS 1.3)

At that time, the power of consciousness (citiśakti) is established in its own nature, as it is in the state of isolation (kaivalya). However, while the mind in its state of emergence (vyutthānacitta) exists, although it is [the same], it is not so [established].
How then?
Because its object has been presented.
In other cases, there is conformity with the mental modifications.

In the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*), those fluctuations of the mind are not distinct from the fluctuations of the *puruṣa*. And thus says the Sūtra: "The seeing is one alone; the seeing is nothing but manifestation (*khyāti*). The mind, like a magnet, assists by its mere proximity and becomes the object of perception for the Lord, the *puruṣa*. Therefore, the cause of the *puruṣa*'s awareness of the mental fluctuations is the beginningless connection (*saṃbandha*). 1.4
Furthermore, those fluctuations of the mind which are to be restrained, being manifold, are fivefold and are either afflicted or unafflicted. (YS 1.5)

Those [mental modifications] caused by the afflictions (*kleśa*), which serve as the field for the accumulation of the latent deposits of karma (*karmāśaya*), are afflicted (*kliṣṭa*). Those whose objects are discriminative discernment (*khyāti*) and which oppose the mandate of the *guṇas* are unafflicted (*akliṣṭa*). Even those falling within the stream of the afflicted are unafflicted; likewise, even amidst gaps in the afflicted, there are unafflicted ones, and amidst gaps in the unafflicted, there are afflicted ones. Mental formations (*saṃskāra*) of such a nature are produced by the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) themselves, and by those mental formations...
Perception, inference, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition.

Perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which is a mental modification (*vṛtti*) primarily characterized by the determination of the specific qualities of an object—consisting of both general and particular aspects—that arises from the coloring of the mind by external things through the channel of the sense organs. Its result (*phala*) is the unqualified awareness of that mental modification by the Puruṣa.
We shall establish later on that the Puruṣa is the experiencer.

Inference (*anumāna*) is a cognitive operation whose primary function is the ascertainment of a universal (*sāmānya*), which has as its object a relationship that follows after things of the same class as the object of inference (*anumeya*) and is excluded from things of a different class. For example: "The moon and stars possess motion because they reach another location, like Caitra;

and the Vindhya mountain lacks motion because it does not reach [another location]. A matter perceived or inferred by a reliable person (*āpta*) is taught through words to others for the purpose of transferring one's own understanding.

The mental modification (*vṛtti*) of a listener that has as its object the meaning of a word is *āgama* (verbal testimony). That *āgama* is subject to error (*plavate*) when the speaker’s words are untrustworthy and his meaning is not perceived or inferred by him. However, if the original speaker has perceived or inferred the meaning, it would be free from error. 1.8 Error (*viparyaya*) is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) which is not established in the actual form of the object.

Why is that not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? Because it is sublated by a valid means of knowledge, since a valid means of knowledge has as its object a thing as it truly is (*bhūtārtha*). In this regard, the sublation of an invalid means of knowledge by a valid one is observed; for example, the perception of two moons is sublated by the perception of one moon, which corresponds to the actual state of affairs. This ignorance (*avidyā*) consists of five links: ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live—these are the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Thus, these very [afflictions] are designated by their own names as *tamas*, *moha*, *mahāmoha*, *tāmisra*, and *andhatāmisra*. These will be discussed in connection with the impurities of the mind. 1.8:
Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is that which follows upon the knowledge of words and is devoid of a real object. *Yogasūtra* 1.9.

It neither conforms to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor does it conform to error (*viparyaya*). Even though it is devoid of a real object (*vastuśūnyatva*), a linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) is observed based on the power of verbal cognition. For example: "Consciousness (*caitanya*) is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the person (*puruṣa*). When consciousness itself is the person, then what is being designated here by what?

Furthermore, there is usage [of words] in reference to designations, as in "Caitra’s cow. Likewise, in the case of "the person is inactive, having the property of a negated entity," or "the arrow stands, will stand, has stood," when the cessation of motion occurs, only the meaning of the verbal root is understood. Similarly, in the statement "the person has the property of non-arising," only the absence of the property of arising is apprehended, not a property inherent to the person. Therefore, that property is conceptually constructed, and through it, linguistic convention exists. 1.9
Sleep is a mental modification whose object is the notion of non-existence.

And that [cognition] is a specific type of mental state (pratyaya-viśeṣa) because it is subject to reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa) upon awakening. How so? "I slept happily; my mind was clear; it makes my wisdom confident. "I slept painfully;
my mind was sluggish, wandering, and unstable; I slept in a deep stupor. "My [limbs were] heavy..."

"My limbs are heavy; my mind is weary; it remains sluggish, as if stolen away. This indeed would not be the reflective awareness of one who has awakened, were there no experience of the mental modification (*pratyaya*); nor would there be the memories dependent upon it regarding that object. Therefore, sleep is a specific kind of mental modification. And it, like other modifications, must be restrained during meditative absorption (*samādhi*). 1.10
Memory is the non-loss of an experienced object.

Does the cognition remember the cognition itself, or rather the object? The cognition, colored by the object to be grasped (*grāhya*), manifests in the form of both the object to be grasped and the act of grasping, and it initiates a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of that same nature. That impression, when activated by its own manifestor, produces a memory consisting of both the object to be grasped and the act of grasping, having that very same form. In this regard, the cognition is preceded by the form of the act of grasping, whereas the memory is preceded by the form of the object to be grasped. And that memory is twofold: that in which the object to be remembered has been cultivated, and that in which it has not.
And there is that which is not cultivated and remembered. In a dream, it is cultivated and remembered; at the time of waking, however, it is not cultivated and remembered.

All memories arise from the experience of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), error (*viparyaya*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), sleep (*nidrā*), and memory (*smṛti*). And all these fluctuations (*vṛtti*) consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion (*moha*). Pleasure, pain, and delusion are to be explained among the afflictions (*kleśa*). That which underlies pleasure...
Attachment is passion (*rāga*); aversion (*dveṣa*) is that which underlies suffering; and delusion (*moha*) is, moreover, ignorance (*avidyā*). All these fluctuations (*vṛtti*) must be restrained.
Upon their restraint, there occurs either cognitive (*saṃprajñāta*) or non-cognitive (*asaṃprajñāta*) meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
1.11 Now, what is the means for their restraint?
Their cessation is achieved through practice and dispassion.

The river of the mind flows in two directions: it flows toward the auspicious and it flows toward the evil. That which is inclined toward isolation (*kaivalya*) and slopes toward the object of discrimination (*viveka*) is the one that flows toward the auspicious. That which is inclined toward worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) and slopes toward the object of non-discrimination is the one that flows toward the evil. Therein, by means of dispassion (*vairāgya*), the stream of sense-objects is made desolate; by the practice of the vision of discrimination, the stream of discrimination is opened.
Thus, the cessation of mental fluctuations depends on both [internal and external means]. 1.12 Practice is the effort toward stability therein. 1.13.

Stability is the tranquil flow of the mind when it is free from fluctuations. Effort for that purpose is vigor, which is enthusiasm. Practice is the performance of the means to achieve that, with the desire to bring it to completion. (1.13) But that [practice], when cultivated over a long period of time, without interruption, and with devotion, becomes firmly grounded. (1.14)

When practiced for a long time, practiced without interruption, and practiced with reverence, and when accomplished through austerity, celibacy, knowledge, and faith, it becomes honored and firm in its foundation. This means that by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the state of emergence, the object [of the mind] is not immediately overwhelmed. 1.14 Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the consciousness of mastery in one who is free from thirst for objects seen or heard of in tradition. *Yogasūtra* 1.15.

Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the state of mastery characterized by effortless spontaneity, devoid of notions of what is to be rejected or accepted; it arises through the power of discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*) in one who perceives the defects of sense-objects, even when in contact with divine or non-divine objects—whether they be women, food and drink, or power in the realm of the seen, or the attainment of heaven, liberation from the body, and absorption into primordial nature in the realm of the heard. (1.15)
That supreme state is dispassion toward the *guṇas*, following the discernment of the *puruṣa*.

One who perceives the defects in objects seen or heard becomes dispassionate; through the practice of perceiving the Puruṣa, his intellect is nourished by the discernment resulting from that purity, and he becomes dispassionate toward the *guṇas*, which possess the nature of both the manifest and the unmanifest. These two constitute dispassion (*vairāgya*). Of these, the latter is merely the clarity of knowledge. Upon its arising, the yogi, having attained discriminative discernment (*khyāti*), thinks thus: "That which was to be attained has been attained."
The afflictions (*kleśa*) that were to be exhausted have been exhausted;

the transition through existence (*bhava-saṃkrama*), with its knotted joints, has been severed—that uninterrupted flow by which, having been born, one dies, and having died, one is born again. Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the supreme culmination of knowledge itself. For isolation (*kaivalya*) is the invariable concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*) of this very state. 1.16

Now, how is it said that for one whose mental fluctuations have been restrained by the two means, there is "cognitive" (saṃprajñāta) samādhi?—it is cognitive because it is accompanied by the forms of reasoning (vitarka), deliberation (vicāra), bliss (ānanda), and the sense of self (asmitā). (YS 1.17)

Vitarka is the gross engagement of the mind with an object; vicāra is the subtle [engagement]. Ānanda is joy. Asmitā is the consciousness of oneness. Among these, the first samādhi, which is accompanied by all four, is savitarka (with vitarka). The second, devoid of vitarka, is savicāra (with vicāra). The third, devoid of vicāra, is sānanda (with ānanda). The fourth, devoid of those [three], is asmitāmātra (mere I-am-ness). All [of these are samprajñāta samādhis].

These are the concentrations with an object. 1.17 Now, as for the concentration without cognitive awareness (asaṃprajñāta-samādhi): what is its means, or what is its nature?—the other [concentration] is preceded by the practice of the cognition of cessation and has residual mental impressions (saṃskāra) remaining. YS 1.18.

When all fluctuations have subsided, the cessation of the mind, in which only latent impressions remain, is *asaṃprajñāta* samādhi. The means to attain it is supreme detachment (*para-vairāgya*). Since practice directed toward an object is not suitable for its accomplishment, the "cessation of mental activity" (*virāma-pratyaya*), which is devoid of an object, is made the object of focus. That [cessation] is empty of any referent; for by means of practice directed toward that, the mind becomes objectless.

It becomes as if it has reached non-existence; this is seedless samādhi, which is without cognitive awareness (asaṃprajñāta). This indeed is of two kinds: that based on means (upāyapratyaya) and that based on existence (bhavapratyaya). Among these, the one based on means belongs to yogins; the one based on existence belongs to those who are dissolved in the body-less [state] or in primordial matter (videhaprakṛtilaya). 1.19.

For the gods of the Videhas, existence is conditioned by their own latent impressions (*bhava-pratyaya*). For they, experiencing as it were the state of isolation (*kaivalya*) through a mind that employs only its own latent impressions, pass away their particular ripening of those impressions. Likewise, those absorbed in primordial nature (*prakṛti-layas*) experience as it were the state of isolation when the mind, still possessing a capacity for action (*sādhikāra*), has dissolved into primordial nature.
Until the mind no longer returns by virtue of its latent predispositions (adhikāra).
1.20 For others, [the attainment of samādhi] is preceded by faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

Skillful means (*upāya*) becomes the condition for yogis. Faith (*śraddhā*) is the clarity of the mind; for it protects the yogi like a virtuous mother. For one who possesses faith and seeks discernment (*viveka*), vigor (*vīrya*) arises. For one in whom vigor has arisen, mindfulness (*smṛti*) is established. When mindfulness is established, the mind, free from agitation, becomes concentrated (*samādhi*). For one whose mind is concentrated...

Discriminative discernment (*prajñāviveka*) arises by which one knows the object as it truly is. Through the practice of that [discernment] and through detachment from its respective objects, *asaṃprajñāta* (non-cognitive) *samādhi* occurs. 1.20 Indeed, those nine types of yogins possess mild, middling, or intense means (*upāya*). Namely: the one with mild means, the one with middling means...

"Superior means" (adhimātropāya). Among these, weak means (mṛdūpāya) is threefold: weak intensity (mṛdu-saṃvega), middling intensity (madhya-saṃvega), and intense intensity (tīvra-saṃvega). Likewise for middling means and likewise for superior means. Among those with superior means—those with intense intensity—the [attainment] is near. (YS 1.21)
The attainment of samādhi and the fruit of samādhi occur;
moreover, there is a distinction [in their intensity] due to being weak, middling, or intense. (YS 1.22)

[The degrees of intensity are] mild-intense, medium-intense, and supreme-intense. There is a distinction even beyond that. Due to that distinction, for one with mild-intense urgency (*saṃvega*), the attainment of concentration (*samādhi*) and its fruit are near; for one with medium-intense urgency, they are nearer; and for one with supreme-intense urgency and supreme means (*upāya*), the attainment of concentration and its fruit are nearest of all. Is it only by this [intensity of urgency] that concentration becomes nearest? Or, in its attainment, is there some other means as well, or not?
Or [samādhi is attained] from devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna). YS 1.23.

The Lord, being won over by [the yogi's] resolve and exceptional devotion, favors him through mere contemplation (*abhidhyāna*). From that mere contemplation, for the yogi, the attainment of samādhi and the fruit of samādhi become exceedingly near. (1.23) Now, who is this so-called Lord (*īśvara*) distinct from *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa*?
The Lord is a distinct Puruṣa, untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, or latent dispositions.

Ignorance and the other afflictions (*kleśa*) are the defilements. Wholesome and unwholesome actions are karma. Their fruition is maturation (*vipāka*). The latent impressions (*vāsanā*) corresponding to those [fruits] are the dispositions (*āśaya*). Although these reside in the mind (*manas*), they are designated as belonging to the *puruṣa*, for he is the enjoyer of their fruit. Just as victory or defeat, though occurring among the warriors, is attributed to the master; likewise, that particular *puruṣa* who is untouched by this experience has attained isolation (*kaivalya*). Indeed, there are many such isolated ones (*kevalin*), for they have severed the three bonds.

Those who have attained isolation (kaivalya) have had no prior connection with Īśvara, nor will they have any future connection. Just as for one who is liberated, a prior limit of bondage is known, it is not so for Īśvara. Or, just as for one merged in primordial nature (prakṛti), a future limit of bondage is conceivable, it is not so for Īśvara. He is eternally liberated and eternally the Lord.
Is that eternal excellence of Īśvara, which arises from his appropriation of a preeminent *sattva*, caused by something or is it without cause? His scripture (*śāstra*) is its cause.
But what is the cause of the scripture?
It has as its cause a preeminent *sattva*.

The relationship between these two—the excellence of scripture and the existence of God—is beginningless. From this it follows that God is eternally so and eternally liberated. Furthermore, His sovereignty is devoid of both equality and superiority.
To begin with, His sovereignty cannot be surpassed by any other sovereignty; for whatever might surpass it would itself be that very sovereignty. Therefore...
He in whom the attainment of the limit of sovereignty resides is the Lord (*īśvara*). And there is no sovereignty equal to His. Why?

Because when two equals simultaneously desire the same object—thinking, "Let this be new" and "Let this be old"—if one succeeds, the other's power of will (*prākāmya*) is frustrated, which results in his inferiority. Furthermore, the simultaneous attainment of the desired object for two equals [is impossible].

It does not exist, because its object is contradictory. Therefore, he alone is the Lord whose sovereignty is free from both equality and superiority; and he is a particular kind of spirit (puruṣaviśeṣa).
Furthermore—
In that state, there exists the unsurpassed seed of omniscience.

This—the apprehension of the past, future, and present, individually and collectively, as well as that which is beyond the senses, whether small or great—is the seed of omniscience (*sarvajñabīja*). As this seed increases until it reaches its ultimate limit, he in whom it is unsurpassed is the omniscient one. There is a reaching of the limit of the seed of omniscience because it possesses degrees of excellence, just like physical magnitude. He in whom there is the reaching of the limit of knowledge is the omniscient one.
And that [person] is a specific individual (*puruṣaviśeṣa*).

Furthermore, since inference, once its function is exhausted by establishing a mere generality (*sāmānyamātra*), is not capable of apprehending a specific detail, the apprehension of his specific name and so forth must be sought from scripture (*āgama*). Even though there is no benefit for oneself in that regard, there is benefit for living beings.
The purpose [of this work] is as follows: "By means of the instruction on knowledge and dharma, I shall rescue transmigrating beings during the dissolution of the eons and the great dissolution.

And so it has been said: "The primordial Knower, the Blessed One, the supreme Sage, having presided over a mind of emanation, out of compassion taught the Tantra to Āsuri, who was desirous of knowing it. (1.25)
This very one is the teacher even of the ancients, because he is not limited by time. (YS 1.26)

For previous teachers are delimited by time; he, however, to whom time does not apply for the sake of delimitation, is the teacher even of those predecessors. Just as he was perfected through the attainment of excellence at the beginning of this creation, so too should he be understood to have been perfected at the beginnings of all past creations. 1.26
The syllable *praṇava* is its designator.

The Lord is the denotable object of the *praṇava*. Is its status as denotable and denoter created by convention (*saṃketa*), or is it established like the light of a lamp? The relationship between this denotable object and its denoter is already established; convention merely manifests that which is already established in the Lord. Just as the relationship between father and son, being as it is, is made manifest by convention:
"This is his father."

"This is his son. Even in other creations (*sarga*), the convention (*saṃketa*) is established in exactly the same way, depending upon the capacity of the signifier and the signified. Because of the permanence of this common understanding, the traditionalists (*āgaminaḥ*) assert that the relationship between word and meaning is eternal.
[This applies] to the yogi who has understood the nature of the signifier and the signified—
The repetition of that [mantra] and the contemplation of its meaning.

The repetition of the *praṇava* and the contemplation of the Lord who is designated by the *praṇava*: for this yogin who repeats the *praṇava* and contemplates the meaning of the *praṇava*, the mind becomes one-pointed.
And so it has been said:
"From self-study one should proceed to yoga; from yoga one should return to self-study."
“Through the perfection of self-study and yoga, the Supreme Self is revealed.
(1.28) Furthermore, what happens for him?
“From that comes the realization of the inward-facing consciousness and the absence of obstacles. (YS 1.29)

First, those obstacles such as disease and the like do not occur for one who is devoted to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna). There also arises for him a vision of his own true nature. Just as the Lord is a Puruṣa—pure, serene, absolute, and free from afflictions—so too does he attain that Puruṣa who is the witness of the intellect (buddhi-pratisaṃvedin). 1.29

Now, what are the obstacles which are the distractions of the mind? Furthermore, what are they and how many are they?—Illness, languor, doubt, negligence, laziness, lack of renunciation, erroneous perception, failure to attain a stage [of concentration], and instability; these distractions of the mind are the obstacles. (YS 1.30)

There are nine intermediate obstacles that cause distraction of the mind; these occur together with the fluctuations of the mind. In their absence, the previously mentioned fluctuations of the mind do not arise. Disease is an imbalance of the bodily humors, fluids, and organs. Lethargy is the mind’s lack of functional readiness. Doubt is a cognition that touches upon two alternatives, [thinking] "it might be thus" or "it might not be thus. Negligence...

The non-cultivation of the means for achieving meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Laziness is the lack of engagement due to heaviness of body and mind. Non-restraint is the greed consisting of the mind’s association with sense objects. Erroneous vision is inverted cognition (*viparyaya-jñāna*). Not having attained the stage is the failure to obtain the stage of meditative concentration. Instability is the mind’s failure to remain fixed once that stage has been obtained. Regarding the attainment of meditative concentration...

For if [the mind] were to exist [in that state], it would remain fixed therein. These nine distractions of the mind are called the impurities of yoga, the opposites of yoga, and the obstacles to yoga. 1.30 Pain, mental distress, trembling of the limbs, and labored inhalation and exhalation are concomitants of distraction. (YS 1.31)

Suffering (*duḥkha*) is that which is internal, external, and celestial; it is that by which living beings are struck and strive for its removal. Mental distress (*daurmanasya*) is the agitation of the mind resulting from the frustration of one's desires. Bodily tremor (*aṅgamejayatva*) is that which makes the limbs quiver and shake. Inhalation (*śvāsa*) is when the breath draws in external air. Exhalation (*praśvāsa*) is that which [expels] the abdominal air.

The expulsion of the air is exhalation (*praśvāsa*). These [distractions] coexist with distraction; they occur for one whose mind is distracted, but they do not occur for one whose mind is concentrated (*samāhita*). Now, since these distractions are the adversaries of concentration (*samādhi*), they must be suppressed by those very two: practice (*abhyāsa*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*). In this regard, while defining the scope of practice, he says this:
To prevent that, there is the practice of a single principle (ekatattvābhyāsa). YS 1.32.

For the purpose of preventing distraction, one should practice the mind by taking hold of a single principle (*ekatattva*). However, for one who holds that the mind consists merely of momentary cognitions restricted to each respective object, every state of mind would be one-pointed and there would be no such thing as a distracted mind at all.
If, on the other hand, this [mind] is withdrawn from everything and concentrated upon a single object, then it becomes one-pointed.
Therefore, [the mind] is not restricted to each respective object.

Furthermore, for one who considers the mind to be one-pointed through a stream of similar cognitions: if that one-pointedness is a property (*dharma*) of the "stream-mind," then no such single stream-mind exists, because of its momentariness. Or, if it is a property of each individual cognition that constitutes a part of the stream, [then...]

Whether that [stream of consciousness] consists of a flow of similar cognitions or a flow of dissimilar cognitions, it is necessarily one-pointed because it is restricted to each respective object; thus, a distracted mind is impossible. Therefore, the mind is a single entity, manifold in its objects, and stable.
Furthermore, if cognitions—distinct by nature—were to arise without being connected to a single mind, then how could one [cognition] remember what was seen by another cognition?

[The agent] would be one thing, and [the experiencer] would be another. Furthermore, the accumulation of the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) by one set of causal conditions (*pratyaya*) would have a different set of causal conditions as its experiencer.
Even if this were somehow reconciled, it would invoke the "logic of cow-dung and milk-porridge" (*gomayapāyasīyanyāya*).
Moreover, if the mind (*citta*) were something other [than the self], it would result in the denial of the experience of one's own self. How so?

The cognition "I" arises as non-different within the cognizer, even though there is a difference between all cognitions, based on the thought: "What I saw, that I touch; and what I touched, that I see. How can this cognition "I," which has a single cognition as its object and is of a non-different nature, exist with respect to mental states that are absolutely distinct, [if it were not] a single common cognizer?

One should take recourse [to this]. And this cognition of "I," whose nature is non-differentiation, is to be grasped through one's own experience. Furthermore, the majesty of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not overridden by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); rather, it is precisely through the power of direct perception that another means of valid cognition obtains its practical application (*vyavahāra*).
Therefore, the mind (*citta*) is one, manifold in its objects, and stable. 1.32
Regarding that state of mind for which this preparatory cultivation is prescribed by the treatise, how is it so?
"By the cultivation of friendliness, compassion, joy, and equanimity toward objects that are happy, suffering, virtuous, and non-virtuous, there is the clarification of the mind. (YS 1.33)

In this regard, one should cultivate loving-kindness toward all living beings who are experiencing happiness; compassion toward those who are suffering; sympathetic joy toward those whose nature is merit; and equanimity toward those whose conduct is non-meritorious. As he cultivates in this way, pure qualities arise within him. Consequently, his mind becomes serene; being serene, it becomes one-pointed and attains a state of stability. 1.33
Or, [the mind becomes one-pointed] by means of exhalation and retention of the breath.

The upward expulsion of the abdominal air through the nostrils by means of a specific effort is *vamana* (vomiting), and its retention is *prāṇāyāma* (breath control); by these two, one may achieve steadiness of the mind.
Or, an activity of the mind directed toward an object that has arisen serves as a basis for steadiness of the mind. (YS 1.34–35)
For one who concentrates on the tip of the nose, that consciousness of divine fragrance is the functioning of smell; on the tip of the tongue, the consciousness of taste;

on the palate, the consciousness of form; in the middle of the tongue, the consciousness of touch; and at the root of the tongue, the consciousness of sound—these functions, once arisen, bind the mind to stability.

They dispel doubt and serve as the gateway to concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). By this it should be understood that the activity arising with respect to the moon, the sun, planets, jewels, lamps, rays of light, and so forth, possesses an object (*viṣayavatī*), even though [it occurs] through those respective scriptures, inference, and the instructions of teachers.
The reality of an object, once understood, becomes truly existent because these [means of knowledge] possess the capacity to demonstrate the object exactly as it is.
Nevertheless, as long as even a single part is not personally experienced through one's own instruments of cognition, the whole remains as if beyond perception;
thus, regarding subtle matters such as liberation, it does not produce a firm conviction. Therefore, for the purpose of corroborating the scriptures, inference, and the instructions of the teacher—

Thus, a certain specific object must necessarily be made directly perceptible. When one portion of that taught object has been perceived, then everything—even subtle objects—can be trusted until final liberation (*apavarga*). It is for this very purpose that this mental cultivation (*cittaparikarma*) is prescribed; it becomes effective once the notion of mastery (*vaśīkārasaṃjñā*) regarding those objects has arisen amidst the fluctuating states of mind.

"It may be for the sake of directly perceiving each respective object. And this being so, his faith, energy, mindfulness, and concentration will proceed without obstruction. 1.36 Or [the samādhi] is "joyless" (*viśoka*) or "luminous" (*jyotiṣmatī*). YS 1.36.

The phrase "an activity has arisen that serves as a basis for the stability of the mind" carries over [from the previous sūtra]. For one who holds [the mind] within the lotus of the heart, there is a consciousness of the intellect (*buddhi-saṃvit*); for the *sattva* of the intellect is luminous and like space.

Due to proficiency in remaining steady therein, the activity [of the mind] is differentiated into the forms of the light of the sun, moon, planets, and jewels. Likewise, [it occurs] in the case of the sense of "I-am-ness" (*asmitā*).
The mind, having attained meditative absorption, becomes like a great ocean without waves—tranquil, infinite, and consisting of pure *asmitā* (I-am-ness).
Regarding this, it has been said: "Having realized that self which is subtle as an atom, one perceives it thus: 'I am.
This twofold state is free from sorrow and possesses an object.

The activity consisting of mere I-consciousness (*asmitāmātrā*) is called "luminous" (*jyotiṣmatī*), by which the yogi’s mind attains a state of stability. Or, the mind has as its object one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*). (YS 1.37)
Or, the yogi’s mind, colored by an object that is a mind free from passion, attains a state of stability. Or, it has as its object the cognition of dreaming or deep sleep. (YS 1.38)

Or, the yogi’s mind, having as its object either the cognition of a dream or the cognition of sleep, attains a state of stability in that very form. Or [stability is attained] through meditation on whatever is desired. (YS 1.39)
One should meditate on whatever is desired. Having attained stability therein, one attains the state of stability elsewhere as well.
1.39 Its mastery extends from the smallest atom to the infinitely great. // YS_1.40 //

For one who enters into the subtle, the point of stability for the mind is reached at the ultimate limit of the atom; for one who enters into the gross, the point of stability for the mind is at the ultimate limit of the infinitely great. Thus, that lack of obstruction which belongs to this [mind] as it pursues both these extremes is the supreme mastery. Through that mastery, the mind of the yogi becomes perfected and no longer requires the preparatory cultivation produced by practice. 1.40
Now, as to what the nature and object of the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) are for the mind that has attained stability, it is said:

"For one whose fluctuations have ceased, like a well-refined gem, there is the meditative attainment which consists in being established in and colored by the grasper, the grasping, and the graspable" (YS 1.41).
"Of one whose fluctuations have ceased" means that for whom all cognitive impressions (*pratyaya*) have subsided. "Like a well-bred gem" is the introduction of an illustration.

Just as a crystal, colored by various proximate objects due to their differences, appears in the form and shape of those proximate objects, so too the mind, colored by the object of perception (*grāhya*), having attained identity with the object, appears in the form and shape of the perceived object itself. [This applies when it is] colored by the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*).

When it has attained identity with a subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*), it takes on the appearance of the essential nature of that subtle element. Likewise, when colored by a gross object of perception, it attains identity with a gross form and takes on the appearance of a gross form. Similarly, when colored by the diversity of the universe, it attains identity with the diversity of the universe and takes on the appearance of the universal form.

The same should be understood regarding the instruments of perception (*grahaṇa*) and the sense organs (*indriya*) as well. When colored by the object of perception (*grahaṇālambana*), it becomes absorbed in that perception and manifests in the form of the very nature of that perception. Likewise, when colored by the person who perceives (*grahītṛpuruṣālambana*), it becomes absorbed in that perceiving person and manifests in the form of the very nature of that perceiving person. Similarly, when colored by the liberated person (*muktapuruṣālambana*), it becomes absorbed in that liberated person...

"It manifests in the form of the essential nature of the liberated *puruṣa*. Thus, when the mind—which is like a noble gem—is directed toward the grasper, the instruments of grasping, and the grasped (which consist of the *puruṣa*, the senses, and the elements), that state of being colored by them while abiding within them—that is, the assumption of their form—is called "attainment" (*samāpatti*). 1.41 Among these, the attainment mixed with the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of word, object, and knowledge is "with deliberation" (*savitarka*). YS 1.42.

For example, the word "cow," the object "cow," and the cognition "cow" are observed to be grasped as undifferentiated, even though they are distinct. When analyzed, however, the properties of the word are one thing, the properties of the object another, and the properties of the cognition another;
thus, their paths are separate. In that regard, for the yogin who has attained meditative absorption, whatever object such as a cow appears within the wisdom (*prajñā*) of samādhi—

If, having ascended [to that state], it returns permeated by the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of words, objects, and knowledge, that mixed attainment is called "with deliberation" (*savitarka*).

However, when, upon the purification of the memory of linguistic conventions, there is the wisdom of meditative concentration (*samādhi-prajñā*) which is devoid of the conceptual constructions of knowledge derived from scripture or inference—

An object situated in its own essential nature is delimited solely by that very form of its own nature; this is the *nirvitarka* (non-discursive) meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). This is supreme perception (*pratyakṣa*), and it is the seed of verbal testimony (*śruta*) and inference (*anumāna*). From it, verbal testimony and inference arise. Furthermore, that vision does not coexist with the cognitions of verbal testimony and inference; therefore, it is unmixed with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

"The vision of the yogi arises from the concentration free from discursive thought (*nirvitarka-samādhi*). The definition of this state of absorption free from discursive thought is illuminated by the Sūtra:
"When memory is purified, [the mind] appears as the object alone, as if devoid of its own form; this is *nirvitarka*. (YS 1.43)

That wisdom (*prajñā*), purified of the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arising from hearing the linguistic conventions and inference, which is colored by the nature of the object of apprehension (*grāhya-svarūpa-uparakta*), abandons its own nature as an act of grasping as if it were itself, and becomes the mere nature of the thing (*padārtha-mātra-svarūpā*), having as it were assumed the very form of the object of apprehension— that is then the *nirvitarka* attainment.
And thus it has been explained: "The object of a single cognition—whether it be a cow, a jar, or any other worldly thing—is indeed composed of a specific accumulation of atoms.
This specific configuration is a common property of the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), inherent to them, and inferred by its manifested effect;
it becomes manifest when its own manifestor appears, and it disappears upon the arising of another property, such as the potsherds. That...

This dharma is called the "whole" (*avayavin*). That which is one, large, minute, tangible, characterized by activity, and impermanent—it is by means of that whole that worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) are carried out. For one [who holds the opposite view], however, that specific aggregation (*pracaya-viśeṣa*) is without a real entity (*avastuka*); and the subtle cause is unperceivable by one who is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*).

Since that [object] lacks a whole (*avayavin*), it follows that for the most part everything is merely false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) because it is not established in its true form. And in that case, what would even right cognition (*samyagjñāna*) be, given the absence of an object? Whatever is perceived is traditionally taught as being a whole; therefore, there exists a whole which has entered into common usage through such qualities as magnitude (*mahattva*). This is due to meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
It becomes the object of the [samādhi] free from vitarka. 1.43 By this very [explanation], the [samādhis] with vicāra and free from vicāra, which have subtle objects, are explained. 1.44.

In that regard, the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) directed toward the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), whose properties (*dharma*) have become manifest and which are delimited by the experience of place, time, and cause, is called "with deliberation" (*savicārā*). There too, it is precisely the subtle element— characterized by the manifested property and apprehended by a single cognition—
that becomes the objective support (*ālambana*) and presents itself within the wisdom (*prajñā*) of samādhi.

Furthermore, that meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) which occurs in relation to all things— whether they are quiescent, arisen, or indeterminate, undivided, following after all phenomena, and consisting of the nature of all phenomena— is called "without deliberation" (*nirvicārā*). For the subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*), being of such a nature,
when it becomes the object of focus in this very form, colors the nature of the wisdom (*prajñā*) of samādhi itself.

And when wisdom (*prajñā*) becomes as if empty of its own nature and consists of the object alone, it is then called "without deliberation" (*nirvicārā*). In that regard, [wisdom] having a gross object is "with verbalization" (*savitarkā*) and "without verbalization" (*nirvitarkā*); [wisdom] having a subtle object is "with deliberation" (*savicārā*) and "without deliberation" (*nirvicārā*). Thus, by this very [state of] being without verbalization, the abandonment of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) for both [types of wisdom] is explained. 1.44 And the state of having subtle objects culminates in the unmanifest (*aliṅga*). 1.45.

The subtle object of the earthy atom is the subtle element of smell; that of the watery, the subtle element of taste; that of the fiery, the subtle element of form; that of the airy, the subtle element of touch; and that of the ethereal, the subtle element of sound. Of these, the ego (ahaṃkāra) is the subtle object.

For this [ego] as well, the subtle object is the "merely indicative" (liṅgamātra). And for the "merely indicative," the subtle object is the "non-indicative" (aliṅga). There is nothing beyond the non-indicative.

There is something even more subtle than that. [Objection: Is it not true that the *puruṣa* is subtle? [Reply: True; however, the subtlety of the unmanifest (*aliṅga*) is superior to that of the *liṅga*, but such is not the case for the *puruṣa*.
For the *puruṣa* is not the inherent cause (*anvayi-kāraṇa*) of the *liṅga*.

"But it is the cause. Therefore, subtlety in the primary principle (pradhāna) is explained as being beyond all degrees. 1.45 Those very [concentrations] are seeded concentration (sabīja-samādhi). YS 1.46.

Since those four attainments have external objects as their seeds, concentration (*samādhi*) is also "with seed" (*sabīja*). In that regard, concentration is enumerated as being fourfold: with reasoning (*savitarka*) and without reasoning (*nirvitarka*) regarding a gross object, and with reflection (*savicāra*) and without reflection (*nirvicāra*) regarding a subtle object. 1.46.
When there is proficiency in the state without reflection, there is inner clarity (*adhyātmaprasāda*). 1.47.

Vaiśāradya (clarity) is the clear, steady flow of the *sattva* of the intellect— which is luminous by nature and free from the impurities of the veil of impurity— when it is not overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*. When this clarity of the *nirvicāra* (reflectionless) samādhi arises,
then for the yogin there occurs internal serenity (*adhyātmaprasāda*), which is a vivid light of wisdom whose object is the true reality and which does not follow a temporal sequence.

And so it has been said: "Having ascended the clarity of wisdom (*prajñā-prasāda*), the wise man, free from grief, looks upon all grieving people as one standing on a mountain peak looks down upon those on the ground. (YS 2.15) "In that state, wisdom is truth-bearing" (YS 1.48).

The wisdom that arises for one whose mind is concentrated upon that [object] receives the designation "truth-bearing" (*ṛtaṃbhara*). This name is significant in its literal sense, for it bears only truth; therein, not even a trace of erroneous cognition exists. And so it has been said:
"By means of scripture, by inference, and by the savor of the practice of meditation..."
"By cultivating wisdom in three ways, one attains the supreme yoga.
(1.48) Furthermore, that [wisdom]—arising from hearing and inference—has a different object, because its purpose is to discern specific characteristics. (1.49)
Scriptural knowledge (*āgamavijñāna*) has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object. For it is not possible to express a particular (*viśeṣa*) by means of scripture;
why?

Because a word has not been established through convention (*saṃketa*) with respect to a particular. Likewise, inference (*anumāna*) also has only a universal as its object. Where there is attainment...
In this regard, it has been stated that where there is no attainment, there is no movement. Furthermore, the generalization is established through inference.
Therefore, there is no specific [object] that falls within the scope of either scripture or inference.
Nor is there apprehension of this subtle, concealed, or remote entity by means of worldly perception. And not of this...

Since the specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) lacks any other means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*), its existence is apprehended solely by the wisdom of meditative concentration (*samādhiprajñā*). Whether that specific distinction pertains to the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) or to the *puruṣa*, it is therefore a wisdom whose object is distinct from the wisdom derived from scripture (*śruta*) and inference (*anumāna*), because its purpose is to discern that specific distinction. (YS 1.49) Upon the attainment of the wisdom of meditative concentration, a new and ever-fresh impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by that wisdom arises for the yogin.
The impression produced by that [practice] obstructs other impressions. (YS 1.50)

The formative force (*saṃskāra*) produced from concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) obstructs the latent tendency toward the formative forces of emergence (*vyutthāna*). Because the formative forces of emergence are overcome, the conditions (*pratyaya*) arising from them do not occur. When those conditions cease, concentration is established. From that comes the wisdom born of concentration; from that come the formative forces created by wisdom. Thus, a new and ever-new latent tendency toward formative forces arises. And from that, wisdom [arises again].
And therefore, regarding "the formative forces" (*saṃskārāḥ*): how could this excellence of formative forces not render the mind subject to further activity?
Those formative forces produced by wisdom do not make the mind characterized by such activity, because they are the cause for the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Indeed, they cause the mind to desist from its own function; for the activity of the mind culminates in *khyāti* (manifestation). 1.50
Furthermore, what happens for him?
"Upon the cessation of that [citta] as well, because of the cessation of everything, there is seedless samādhi" (YS 1.51).
It is not only an obstacle to concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), but it also acts as a hindrance to the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) produced by wisdom. Why?
Because the formative force born of cessation (*nirodha*) subverts the formative forces born of concentration.

The existence of the formative forces produced by the mind of cessation is to be inferred through the experience of the sequence of time during the duration of that cessation. [This is known] by means of those [forces] arising from the meditative absorption of emergence and the meditative absorption of cessation.
Together with the latent impressions conducive to isolation (*kaivalya*), the mind dissolves into its own primordial nature (*prakṛti*) as it abides therein.

Therefore, those impressions are antagonistic to the mind’s functional mandate; they do not become causes for its continued existence. Because the mind, having completed its mandate, ceases along with the impressions conducive to isolation.
When that [cognitive process] has ceased, the person is established in his own nature alone; therefore, he is called pure, isolated, and liberated.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Samādhi-pāda, in the illustrious Pātañjala Yoga-śāstra, the exposition of Sāṃkhya, with the commentary by the venerable Vyāsa.
Yoga has been described for one whose mind is concentrated. Now this is commenced: how may even one whose mind is in a state of emergence (vyutthita) be joined with yoga?
Austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord constitute the yoga of action (kriyāyoga).

Yoga is not perfected for one who lacks austerity (*tapas*). Since impurity—which is variegated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of beginningless karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) and presented as a web of sense objects—does not undergo dissolution without austerity, austerity is undertaken. And it is held that this [austerity] should be practiced so as not to obstruct the clarity of the mind (*citta-prasādana*).

Self-study (*svādhyāya*) is the recitation of purifying mantras such as the *praṇava*, or the study of the scriptures on liberation. Devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*) is the offering of all actions to the Supreme Teacher, or the renunciation of their fruits. (2.1) For that indeed is the yoga of action: it is for the purpose of cultivating *samādhi* and for the purpose of attenuating the afflictions (*kleśa*). (YS 2.2)

For when that [practice] is cultivated, it develops meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and attenuates the afflictions (*kleśa*). Having attenuated the afflictions, it will render them incapable of further production, like seeds burnt by the fire of discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*). Because of their attenuation, the subtle wisdom—the manifestation of the mere distinction between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, untouched by the afflictions—will have fulfilled its purpose.
"It will serve for the purpose of reversal.
2.2 Now, what are the afflictions (kleśas), and how many are there?—Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live are the afflictions. (YS 2.3)
The "afflictions" (kleśa) mean the five types of error. When they are active, they strengthen the authority of the guṇas,
establish their transformation,
and cause the stream of cause and effect to flow upward.
Having become dependent on mutual assistance, they bring about the ripening of karma. 2.4 Ignorance is the field for the others—whether dormant, attenuated, interrupted, or expansive.

In this context, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the field, the ground of production, for the fourfold varieties of egoism (*asmitā*) and the other [afflictions]—namely, those that are dormant (*prasupta*), attenuated (*tanu*), interrupted (*vicchinna*), and active (*udāra*). Among these, what is dormancy? It is the state of having entered the condition of a seed, remaining in the mind as mere potentiality. Its awakening is the manifestation [of the affliction] toward an object. For one who possesses discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*) and whose seeds of affliction have been burnt, this [awakening] does not occur again, even when an object is present before them.

"How can there be sprouting for a burnt seed? Therefore, one whose afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted is called "virtuous" (*kuśala*) and "in his final body. In that state alone—never elsewhere—is that fifth stage of the afflictions characterized by the condition of burnt seeds. Since the capacity of the seeds of existing afflictions has been burnt, even when an object (*viṣaya*) is present before them, their awakening does not occur; thus, "dormancy" (*prasupti*) has been explained.

And there is the non-sprouting of burnt seeds. "Attenuation" is said as follows: the afflictions (*kleśa*), being struck down by the cultivation of their antidotes, become attenuated. Likewise, they are called "interrupted" because they manifest again and again in various forms after having been repeatedly severed; for instance, since anger is not observed at the time of passion, anger does not manifest at the time of passion. Furthermore, while passion is seen in one place, it is not absent in another object; for example, Caitra may be impassioned toward one woman [but not another].
Thus, one may be detached from other women;
however, in that case, passion has attained its activity toward her, whereas toward others it possesses only a future activity. For at that time, [passion] is dormant, attenuated, or interrupted.

That which has attained its activity toward an object is "intense" (*udāra*). All these indeed do not transcend the state of being objects of the afflictions (*kleśa*). What, then, is an "interrupted," "dormant," "attenuated," or "intense" affliction?
It is said: This is indeed true;

however, it is only these [afflictions] in their specific forms that possess the quality of being interrupted and so forth. Just as one has desisted from the cultivation of the counter-measures, so too has one been manifested by the manifesting agent of its own kind. All these afflictions are merely varieties of ignorance (*avidyā*). Why?

Ignorance alone pervades all [the afflictions]. Whatever object is constructed by ignorance, upon that very thing the afflictions lie latent; they are perceived at the time when there are conditions for error, and as ignorance wanes, they likewise wane.
2.4 Therein, the essential nature of ignorance is stated:
Ignorance (avidyā) is the perception of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in that which is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self. (YS 2.5)
The appearance of permanence in impermanent effects. For example: "The earth is eternal;
the sky, with its moon and stars, is eternal; the dwellers of heaven are immortal. Likewise, regarding the body, which is impure and supremely loathsome—
“Because of its location, its seed, its support, its outflow, and also its end;
and because it must be purified by external application, the wise indeed know the body to be impure.”

Thus, the perception of purity in the impure is observed. [For example: "This lovely girl is like a fresh crescent moon; she seems as if fashioned from the very limbs of honey and nectar, or as if known to have emerged after piercing the moon.
With eyes as wide as the petals of a blue lotus, she seems to comfort the world of the living with her glances full of amorous gestures.

What connection could there be between these things? And yet, such a cognition of purity arises regarding the impure. By this same principle, the cognition of merit in what is demeritorious [is explained].
In the same way, the perception of value in what is valueless has been explained.

Likewise, he will state [later] regarding suffering that it appears as happiness: "To the discerning person, everything is indeed suffering because of the sufferings of transformation, anxiety, and latent impressions, and because of the conflict between the functions of the *guṇas*. In that context, the perception of happiness is ignorance (*avidyā*). Similarly, the perception of a self in what is not-self—

It is the manifestation of the self (*ātma-khyāti*) with respect to what is not the self—whether it be external implements, sentient or insentient, or the body which is the locus of experience, or the mind which is an instrument for the person. Thus it has been said here: "Having perceived a manifest or unmanifest entity (*sattva*) as the self, one rejoices in its prosperity, thinking it to be the prosperity of the self; one grieves over its misfortune, thinking it to be the misfortune of the self."
"Thinking thus, he remains entirely unawakened. This fourfold ignorance is the root of this continuum of afflictions and of the latent deposit of karma along with its maturation.
Its reality as a substantial entity is to be understood like "non-friend" or "non-cow-track"; just as "non-friend" (amitra) is neither the absence of a friend nor merely a friend.

But its opposite is the adversary (*sapatna*). Just as "non-cow-track" (*agoṣpada*) is neither the absence of a cow-track nor merely a cow-track, but rather a different entity altogether—a specific location—so too, ignorance (*avidyā*) is neither valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor the absence of valid cognition;
rather, ignorance is another form of knowledge that is contrary to knowledge (*vidyā*). 2.5
Asmitā is the apparent identity of the powers of the seer and the seeing.

The *asmitā* affliction is said to be the state where the power of seeing (*dṛk-śakti*), which is the Puruṣa, and the power of seeing (*darśana-śakti*), which is the intellect (*buddhi*), appear as if they have attained a single nature. When there is an apparent non-distinction between the power of the enjoyer and the power of the object of enjoyment—which are absolutely distinct and absolutely unmixed—experience (*bhoga*) is possible. However, when those two regain their own true natures, there is only isolation (*kaivalya*); how [could experience exist then]?

Regarding "objects of enjoyment" (*bhoga*): as it has been said—“Not perceiving the Puruṣa, who is distinct from the intellect (*buddhi*) by virtue of [his] form, character, knowledge, and so forth, one might, through delusion, conceive the notion of a self (*ātma-buddhi*) therein.
(YS 2.6) Attachment (*rāga*) is that which lies latent in pleasure. (YS 2.7)
Attachment (*rāga*) is that greed, thirst, or lust which, for one who has experienced pleasure, is preceded by the recollection of that pleasure and is directed toward pleasure or its means. 2.7.
Hatred (*dveṣa*) is that which lies latent within suffering. 2.8.

Hatred (*dveṣa*) is that aversion, resentment, desire to strike, or anger directed toward suffering or its causes, preceded by the direct cognition of suffering and the recollection of suffering. 2.8. Clinging (*abhiniveśa*) is an instinctive flow of attachment that persists even in the wise man. 2.9.

This self-cherishing wish—“May I not cease to be; may I continue to exist”—is eternal for every living being. And such a wish for one's own self does not arise in one who has not experienced the nature of death. By this, the experience of a previous birth is inferred. Furthermore, this clinging is a defilement that flows by its own natural force; even in a creature just born as a worm, there is a fear of death that cannot be accounted for by perception, inference, or scripture.
Consisting of the view of annihilationism, it leads one to infer the suffering of death experienced in a previous birth.

Just as this affliction is seen even among those who are utterly ignorant, so too is it firmly rooted in the wise person who understands both the prior and subsequent limits [of existence]. Why? Because for both—the virtuous and the non-virtuous—this is a latent impression (*vāsanā*) resulting from the experience of the same suffering of death. (2.9)
These subtle [afflictions] are to be abandoned by re-absorption.

Those five afflictions, resembling burnt seeds, set along with that very mind when the mind has ceased its activity for the practitioner. But for those [afflictions] that remain in the state of seeds— “their fluctuations are to be abandoned by meditation” (YS 2.11).

Those gross manifestations of the afflictions (*kleśa*) are attenuated by the yoga of action (*kriyā-yoga*); once they have been thinned, they are to be abandoned through discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), that is, through meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), until they are rendered subtle, like seeds that have been burnt. Just as the gross dirt on clothes is first shaken off and the fine residue is later removed with effort and skillful means, so too are the afflictions [initially countered] by weak antidotes.

The gross fluctuations [of the mind] belong to the afflictions, while the subtle ones are their great antidotes. 2.11 The latent deposit of karma has its root in the afflictions; it is to be experienced in this life or in a future life. 2.12.

In that regard, the latent deposit of meritorious and non-meritorious karma arises from desire, greed, delusion, and anger. It is both to be experienced in the present life and to be experienced in a future life.

Among these, that which is accomplished through intense fervor by means of mantras, austerity, and meditative absorption, or which is perfected through the propitiation of the Lord, the gods, the great seers, or those of great spiritual power—that deposit of meritorious karma ripens immediately. Likewise, [that which is produced] by intense affliction [ripens immediately].

When harm is repeatedly inflicted upon those who are afraid, diseased, or miserable; or upon those who have placed their trust in one, or upon high-minded ascetics—that latent disposition toward evil karma ripens immediately. Just as the youth Nandīśvara, having abandoned his human form, was transformed into a deity, so too did Nahuṣa, the Indra of the gods, abandon his own form.

"Transformed into the state of an animal. In that regard, for those in the hells, there is no latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) to be experienced in the present life. Furthermore, even for those whose afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted, there is no latent deposit of karma to be experienced in a future life. 2.12 When the root exists, its fruition consists of birth, lifespan, and experience. (YS 2.13)

When the afflictions (*kleśa*) exist, the latent predisposition of karma (*karmāśaya*) becomes capable of producing its fruition (*vipāka*); it does not do so when the root of the afflictions has been severed. Just as rice grains covered by husks are capable of sprouting provided their seed-nature is not burnt, whereas those from which the husks have been removed or whose seed-nature is burnt are not, so too the latent predisposition of karma, enveloped by afflictions, leads to the growth of fruition; it does not do so when the afflictions have been removed, nor when the seed-nature of the afflictions has been burnt away by discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*). And that fruition is threefold: birth, lifespan, and experience.

In this regard, the following is investigated: Is a single action the cause of a single birth, or does a single action project multiple births? This is the second investigation: Do multiple actions bring about multiple births, or do multiple actions bring about a single birth? First of all, a single action is not the cause of a single birth. Why?

Because there would be no fixed order for the ripening of the fruits of the countless remaining karmas accumulated since beginningless time, as well as of present karma, a lack of confidence in the world would follow;
and that is undesirable. Furthermore, a single karma is not the cause of multiple births. Why?
Because if each individual karma among the many were the cause of multiple births, it would follow that there would be no time for the ripening of the remaining karma.

And that [result] would also be undesirable. Furthermore, multiple actions do not constitute the cause for a single birth. Why? Because those multiple births cannot occur simultaneously; they must be said to occur only in succession. And in that case, the aforementioned fault would persist.

Therefore, the diverse accumulation of the latent impressions (*karmāśaya*) of meritorious and non-meritorious actions performed during the interval between birth and death exists in a relationship of primary and secondary importance.
Having established death through a single impulse manifested at the time of departure (*prāyaṇa*), one who has become faint (*saṃmūrchita*) produces only a single birth.

That birth, by that very same karma, becomes one whose lifespan has been obtained; during that lifespan, experience (*bhoga*) is produced by that very same karma. Thus, this latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) is designated as "having threefold fruition" (*trivipāka*), because it is the cause of birth, lifespan, and experience.

Thus it is said that the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) is "belonging to a single birth" (*ekabhavika*). However, that which is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭajanmavedanīya*) initiates either a single fruition (*ekavipākārambhī*), because it is the cause of experience, or it initiates two fruitions (*dvivipākārambhī*), as in the cases of Nandīśvara or Nahuṣa, because it is the cause of both [the body] and experience. But by means of these latent impressions (*vāsanās*)—which are brought about by the experience of the fruition of afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma—...
This mind has been coagulated since beginningless time and is, as it were, variegated, spread out on all sides like a fish-net with knots;

these are the latent dispositions (*vāsanā*) preceded by many births. As for this storehouse of karma (*karmāśaya*), it is said to belong to a single birth. Those formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) which are the causes of memory are the latent dispositions, and they are beginningless.

Now, that latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) which pertains to a single birth is both of determinate fruition and of indeterminate fruition. Among these, this rule applies only to that which is to be experienced in the present life and has determinate fruition, but not to that which is to be experienced in a future life and has indeterminate fruition. Why?

Because for that which is to be experienced in a future life and is of indeterminate fruition, there are three possible courses: [first] the destruction of what has been performed before it has ripened; [second]...
Either there is an entry into the primary karma, or there is a long-term persistence of that which is overwhelmed by a primary karma of fixed ripening.
In this regard, the destruction of what has been done but not yet ripened is as follows: just as here, through the arising of white karma, black karma is destroyed right here. As it is said:

It has been said: "Two types of actions indeed must be known; the single heap of evil deeds destroys [the merit] of the doer of good. Therefore, you should desire to perform well-done deeds; for it is here that the wise declare action to be. This refers to the entry into the primary action. Regarding this, it is said: "There may be a slight mixture [of impurity], which is remediable and tolerable; it is not sufficient to diminish the wholesome. Why? Because..."
"For I have much other merit, into which this [demerit] has entered as a mere addition; it will cause only a slight reduction even in heaven.
Or, there may be a long duration for that which is overwhelmed by a primary karma of certain ripening. How so?
For death is the common cause of manifestation for karma that is of certain ripening and to be experienced in a future birth.

This has been stated; however, it does not apply to karma that is to be experienced in a future life (*adṛṣṭajanmavedanīya*) and whose ripening is indefinite (*aniyatavipāka*). For such karma—karma to be experienced in a future life with indefinite ripening—it may perish, or it may enter into a state of being stored away (*āvāpa*), or it may remain suppressed for a long time, until a corresponding manifesting condition (*abhivyañjaka-nimitta*) brings its ripening toward fruition. This refers specifically to the ripening of that [indefinite] karma.

Because the place, time, and cause [of fruition] cannot be determined, this course of karma is manifold and difficult to understand. Furthermore, the general rule is not set aside by its exceptions; thus, the latent disposition of karma (*karmāśaya*) pertaining to a single birth is acknowledged. 2.13 They have pleasure and pain as their fruits, because they have merit and demerit as their causes. (YS 2.14)

Those births, lifespans, and experiences have happiness as their fruit when caused by merit, and suffering as their fruit when caused by demerit. And just as this suffering is of a contrary nature, so too, even at the time of sensory pleasure, there exists for the yogin a suffering that is of a contrary nature. How is this established? 2.14 [It is established as follows:]—
To the discerning person, everything is indeed suffering because of the sufferings of change, anxiety, and latent impressions, and because of the conflict between the functions of the guṇas. YS 2.15.

Since this experience of pleasure for everyone is permeated by passion (*rāga*) and depends upon means that are either conscious or unconscious, there exists therein a latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) born of passion. Likewise, one hates the instruments of suffering and becomes deluded; thus, there also exists a latent deposit of karma produced by hatred (*dveṣa*) and delusion (*moha*).
And so it has been said: "Since enjoyment is not possible without harming living beings, there also exists a bodily [deposit of karma] produced by violence (*hiṃsā*)."
[This is] the "residue of karma. And it has been stated that sensory pleasure is ignorance (*avidyā*).

That which is the cessation of the thirst of the senses for objects is happiness; that which is the non-cessation [of that thirst] due to greed is suffering. Furthermore, it is not possible to effect the absence of thirst through the repeated practice of enjoyment, because following the repeated practice of enjoyment, passions increase as do the capacities of the senses. Therefore, this is not a means [to liberation].
"The repeated enjoyment of pleasure": indeed, this person who seeks pleasure and is steeped in sense objects is like one bitten by a venomous snake while fearing the poison of a scorpion;
he is submerged in a great mire of suffering. This is what is called "the suffering of transformation" (*pariṇāmaduḥkhatā*); it is adverse and afflicts the yogi even during a state of pleasure.

Now, what is the suffering of pain (*tāpa-duḥkhatā*)? It is the experience of pain, permeated by aversion, which depends upon means that are either conscious or unconscious; therein lies the latent deposit of karma born of aversion. Furthermore, desiring the means of pleasure, one exerts oneself through body, speech, and mind; from that [arises further karma].

One accumulates merit and demerit through the benefit or injury of others, thinking "I am greatly favoring them" or "I am harming them. That latent deposit of karma arises from greed and delusion; this is called the suffering of pain (*tāpa-duḥkhatā*). What, then, is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*)?

From the experience of pleasure, there is a latent deposit of the formation of pleasure; from the experience of pain, there is also a latent deposit of the formation of pain. Thus, while the fruition of karma is being experienced—whether as pleasure or pain—there is again an accumulation of the latent deposit of karma.
Thus, this beginningless stream of suffering, having spread far and wide, causes only the yogi to tremble because its nature is contrary to his state. Why?

Because "the wise man is like the eye-ball. Just as a strand of wool placed upon the eye-ball causes pain through touch but not on other parts of the body, so too these sufferings afflict only the yogi who is like the eye-ball, and not the other ordinary practitioner.

But for the other [the transmigrating being], who is afflicted by his own karma, there arise—whenever he takes up what has been acquired and discards what has been discarded, and discards what has been taken up and acquires what has been discarded—the threefold torments (tāpa) caused by external, internal, and both types of objects, following every birth. These follow him as he is pursued on all sides by ignorance (*avidyā*), which is like a mental fluctuation variegated by beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and as he clings to the notions of "I" and "mine" (*ahaṃkāra-mamakāra*) which are to be abandoned. Thus, through this beginningless process...

Seeing himself and the collection of beings being swept away by the stream of suffering, the yogi takes refuge in right vision (*samyagdarśana*), which is the cause for the destruction of all suffering.

Furthermore, due to the conflict between the functions of the *guṇas*, everything is indeed suffering for the discerning person. The qualities of the intellect (*buddhi*) consist of the forms of illumination, activity, and inertia.
Having become dependent on mutual assistance, they initiate only a three-guṇic cognition—whether peaceful, terrible, or deluded.
And because the functioning of the guṇas is mobile, the mind is said to be subject to rapid transformation. Distinctions of form and distinctions of function are mutually contradictory.

The *sāmānyas* (general qualities), however, function together with the *atiśayas* (specific intensifications). Thus, these *guṇas*, by depending upon one another, produce the notions of pleasure, pain, and delusion; consequently, all of them take on every form.
Their distinction, however, is created by their status as either subordinate (*guṇa*) or predominant (*pradhāna*). Therefore, for the discerning person, everything is indeed suffering.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the seed from which this great mass of suffering arises. And its remedy is right vision (*samyagdarśana*).

The cause by way of non-existence (*abhāvahetu*). For example, the science of medicine consists of four divisions: disease, the cause of disease, health, and the medicine. In the same way, this treatise also consists of exactly four divisions. Namely: cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), the cause of cyclic existence, liberation (*mokṣa*), and the means to liberation. Among these, cyclic existence, which is full of suffering, is that which is to be abandoned (*heya*). The conjunction of primary matter (*pradhāna*) and the spirit (*puruṣa*) is the cause of what is to be abandoned.

The absolute cessation of conjunction is abandonment (*hāna*). The means to abandonment is right vision (*samyagdarśana*). In this regard, the true nature of the abandoner cannot be either something to be acquired or something to be abandoned; for if it were abandoned, there would be the consequence of the doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*), and if it were acquired, there would be the doctrine of causality (*hetuvāda*). By rejecting both [extremes], there is the doctrine of eternalism (*śāśvatavāda*). This is right vision. 2.15
Thus, this treatise is said to consist of four divisions:
that which is to be abandoned is future suffering. (YS 2.16)

Past suffering has already been carried away by experience and thus does not belong to the category of what is to be abandoned. Present suffering, being absorbed in enjoyment during its own moment, does not become something to be abandoned in the subsequent moment. Therefore, it is only future suffering that afflicts the yogi—who is like one holding a bowl of oil—and no other practitioner; that alone becomes the object of abandonment. (2.16)
Therefore, that which is said to be the object of abandonment is precisely its cause that is pointed out:
"The conjunction of the seer and the seen is the cause of what is to be abandoned" (YS 2.17).
The Puruṣa is the seer and the experiencer of the intellect (buddhi). All objects of sight (dṛśya) are the properties (dharmas) mounted upon the substance of the intellect.
This very object of sight, which is like a magnet, assists merely by its proximity and becomes "one's own" to the Puruṣa, who is of the nature of seeing and is the master.

Because it has become the object of the karma of experience; although it has acquired its own nature through another form and is independent, it is dependent because it exists for the sake of another.
