The beginningless conjunction of those two—the powers of seeing and being seen—produced by their mutual purpose, is the cause of that which is to be abandoned, meaning it is the cause of suffering. And so it has been said: "By abandoning the cause of that conjunction, there may be this absolute remedy for suffering. Why?

Because one perceives a remedy for that cause of suffering which is to be avoided. For example: the foot-sole is the object to be pierced, the thorn is the piercer, and the avoidance consists of [placing] the thorn upon the foot.
The basis of giving is that which is shielded by footwear; these three, whoever knows them in this world, when applying a remedy therein, does not experience suffering born of division. Why?
Because of the power of perceiving their triad. Here too, it is *sattva* alone that is tormented by *rajas*, the tormentor. Why?
Because the action of heating resides in the object, the action of heating occurs in the *sattva* as its object, not in the *kṣetrajña*, who is unchanging and inactive;
for [the *kṣetrajña*] has been shown to be the subject [of experience]. However, when the *sattva* is being heated, the *puruṣa* also experiences heat, conforming to the form of that [sattva]. (2.17)

The nature of the object of perception is stated: "The object of perception consists of the elements and the sense organs; its nature is illumination, activity, and inertia; and it exists for the purpose of experience and liberation. (YS 2.18)

Sattva is characterized by luminosity; rajas, by activity; and tamas, by inertia. These qualities (guṇas) have distinct divisions that are mutually colored [by one another], are subject to transformation, possess the properties of conjunction and disjunction, and have acquired their forms through mutual dependence.

Even while serving as mutual limbs to one another, they maintain an undivided distinction of powers, following the differentiation of powers both homogeneous and heterogeneous at the time of the Pradhāna.

Although they are subordinate qualities (*guṇa*), their existence is inferred as being contained within the primary substance (*pradhāna*) through its mere activity; their capacity is impelled by the necessity of fulfilling the purpose of the Spirit (*puruṣārtha*);

they assist by their mere proximity, like a magnet; and following the modification of one [of the three qualities] without requiring a conscious agent, they come to be designated by the term "primary substance" (*pradhāna*). This is what is called the "visible" (*dṛśya*).

This [unmanifest], consisting of the elements and the senses, undergoes transformation into the state of the elements—earth and so forth—in both subtle and gross forms; likewise, it undergoes transformation into the state of the senses—the ear and so forth—in both subtle and gross forms. Furthermore, that [transformation] does not occur without a purpose, but rather proceeds by taking up a purpose; for that object of perception exists for the sake of experience (bhoga) and liberation (apavarga) for the Puruṣa. In this regard, there is the ascertainment of the nature of the qualities (guṇas) as being desirable or undesirable.

Experience is the attainment of non-differentiation [between the self and the intellect], while liberation is the ascertainment of the enjoyer’s own true nature. There is no other doctrine of perception beyond these two. And so it has been said: "But this person, observing all objects as they are presented—whether they belong to the three active *guṇas* or to the inactive *puruṣa*, who is of a different and yet similar class as the fourth, and who stands as the witness of their activity—"
One might suspect that there is something else [besides the Self] which does not perceive.

How is it that these two—enjoyment and liberation—which are produced by the intellect and reside only in the intellect, are attributed to the Puruṣa? It is just as victory or defeat, though occurring among the warriors, is attributed to the master, for he is the enjoyer of their fruit.

Thus, bondage and liberation, though residing only in the intellect (*buddhi*), are attributed to the person (*puruṣa*), for he is the enjoyer of their fruit. Bondage is the non-fulfillment of the purpose of the person within the intellect; liberation is the completion of that purpose. By this, it is shown that apprehension, retention, reasoning, rejection, knowledge of reality, and attachment, though residing in the intellect, [are attributed to the person].
[The Self] is that which has superimposed upon it the existence [of objects]; for it is indeed the enjoyer of their fruit.
Now, this [sūtra] is commenced in order to determine the specific distinctions in the nature of the perceivable guṇas:
"The stages of the guṇas are the specific, the non-specific, the mere-indicative, and the unindicative. (YS 2.19)

In that context, space, air, fire, water, and earth are the specific manifestations (*viśeṣa*) of the non-specific subtle elements (*aviśeṣa*)—namely, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Likewise, the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose are the organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*);
speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals are the organs of action (*karmendriya*);
and the eleventh is the mind (*manas*), which pertains to all objects.

Thus, these are the specific manifestations of the non-specific [state] characterized by the sense of "I" (asmitā). This sixteenfold specific transformation belongs to the guṇas. There are six non-specific [states], namely: the subtle element of sound, the subtle element of touch, the subtle element of form, the subtle element of taste, the subtle element of smell, and the sixth non-specific state, which is the mere sense of "I. These six non-specific transformations belong to the Great Principle (mahat), the self which is pure existence.

That subtle principle (*liṅgamātra*), the great element (*mahattattva*) which arises from the supreme specificities (*paramaviśeṣa*),— having established themselves in that Great Self (*mahat* ātman) consisting of mere existence (*sattāmātra*),

these [specificities] experience the culmination of their growth. And when they are being reabsorbed, having likewise established themselves in that very Great Self consisting of mere existence, they reach that state which is neither existence nor non-existence (*niḥsattāsatta*).

They recognize that Pradhāna as being without existence or non-existence, without manifestation, and without marks (aliṅga). This is their transformation as mere mark (liṅgamātra), and the state of being without marks is the transformation beyond existence and non-existence.
In the state of being without marks, the purpose of the Puruṣa is not the cause; nor does the purpose of the Puruṣa serve as the cause at the beginning of the state of being without marks.

The fact that it serves the purpose of the Puruṣa is not its cause; thus, because it does not produce a purpose for the Puruṣa, it is called "eternal. However, for the three specific states, the fact that they serve the purpose of the Puruṣa is their cause; since that purpose is their cause, motive, ground, and reason, they are called "non-eternal. The Guṇas, however, which follow all phenomena, neither perish nor are they produced.

It is through the individuals themselves—possessing the passing away and coming into being of the past and future, and inhering the qualities—that [the substance] appears as if it were subject to the properties of arising and perishing. Just as one says, "Devadatta is becoming poor; why? Because his cows are dying," the poverty belongs to him solely because of the death of the cows, not because of a loss of his own essential nature; such is the same resolution.

The mere *liṅga* (the subtle body) is proximate to the *aliṅga* (the unmanifest); there, that [unmanifest] is distinguished as being merged within it through the transcendence of the sequence. Likewise, the six *aviśeṣas* (the five tanmātras and *ahaṃkāra*), being merged in the *liṅgamātra*, are distinguished according to the fixed rule of the sequence of transformation. Similarly, the elements and the sense organs, being merged within those *aviśeṣas*, are distinguished.
And so it was stated previously: since there is no other principle beyond the *viśeṣas*, the *viśeṣas* do not undergo transformation into another principle.
However, their transformations of state (*dharma*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and condition (*avasthā*) will be explained.
(2.19) The object of perception has been explained; now this [sūtra] is commenced for the purpose of determining the true nature of the perceiver.
The Seer is pure consciousness alone; though pure, he observes the mental modifications.
"Pure seeing" (*dṛśimātra*) means the power of vision itself, untouched by any qualifications. That *puruṣa* is the perceiver of the intellect (*buddhi*).

It is neither identical with the intellect nor entirely different from it. First, it is not identical; why? Because its objects are both known and unknown, whereas the intellect is subject to transformation (*pariṇāminī*). Its objects—such as cows or jars—are both known and unknown.
This demonstrates its capacity for transformation (*pariṇāmitva*).

However, the fact that the object is always known by the *puruṣa* illuminates the *puruṣa*'s lack of transformation (*apariṇāmitva*). Why? Because it is impossible for the intellect (*buddhi*) to be both the object of the *puruṣa* and [simultaneously] unapprehended and apprehended; thus, the *puruṣa*'s state of having an object that is always known is established.

And therefore, there is non-transformability [of the Puruṣa]. Furthermore, the intellect (*buddhi*) exists for the sake of another because it acts through conjunction; the Puruṣa exists for its own sake. Likewise, the intellect consists of the three *guṇas* because it determines all objects, and because it consists of the three *guṇas*, it is insentient. The Puruṣa, however, is the witness of the *guṇas*; therefore, it is not similar [to the intellect].

Let it then be dissimilar. Why is it not absolutely dissimilar? Because, although pure, it is a "beholder of the mental modification" (*pratyayānupaśya*). It beholds the mental modification belonging to the intellect.

Perceiving that [intellect], although not of its nature, it appears as if it were of its nature. And so it has been said: "The power of the enjoyer (the puruṣa) is indeed unchanging and non-transferrable, yet it appears as if transferred into the changing object; it follows the modifications of that [intellect]. And because it merely imitates the modification of the intellect—which has acquired the form of being assisted by consciousness—the activity of cognition is described as being indistinguishable from the modification of the intellect. (2.20)
The very nature of the object of perception is for that purpose alone.
The object of sight (dṛśya) has attained the state of being an object for the Puruṣa, whose nature is seeing; thus, the very purpose of the object of sight becomes its essence (ātman).

The meaning is that it becomes its own true nature (svarūpa). However, when its purpose—experience and liberation—has been accomplished by the Puruṣa, the object of sight is no longer seen by the Puruṣa in its own nature, having instead acquired its identity through the form of another (the Puruṣa). Because of this loss of its [distinct] nature, its destruction would follow, yet it does not actually perish. (2.21)
Why?
Because, although it has perished for one who has achieved their purpose, it has not perished, since it is common to others. (YS 2.22)

For a single person whose purpose has been fulfilled, the object of sight (*dṛśya*), even though it has perished—that is, even though it has reached destruction—is not destroyed for others, because it is common to other persons. Even though it has reached destruction for a virtuous person, it has not fulfilled its purpose for non-virtuous persons; therefore, it indeed attains the status of being an object of action for their vision. Thus, by means of another's form, it retains its own form. And for this reason, regarding the two powers of seeing and the seen...

It has been explained that conjunction is beginningless because it is eternal. And so it has been said: "Because there is a beginningless conjunction of substrata (dharmin), there is also a beginningless conjunction of mere attributes (dharma). This sūtra was composed with the intention of describing the essential nature of conjunction. 2.22.
Conjunction is the cause for the perception of the essential natures of both the self and its master [the Lord]. (YS 2.23)

The Puruṣa, the master, is conjoined with its own object of vision for the purpose of seeing. From that conjunction, whatever perception of the object occurs is experience (*bhoga*). However, the perception of the seer’s own true nature is liberation (*apavarga*). Since conjunction terminates when the purpose of seeing is fulfilled, seeing is said to be the cause of disjunction. Seeing is the opposite of non-seeing; thus, non-seeing [is the cause of conjunction].

The cause of conjunction has been explained. In this context, vision (*darśana*) is not the direct cause of liberation; rather, the absence of bondage occurs simply through the absence of non-vision (*adarśana*), and that [absence] is liberation. Since the destruction of non-vision—the cause of bondage—occurs when vision is present, vision, which is knowledge (*jñāna*), is said to be the cause of isolation (*kaivalya*).
Furthermore, what is this so-called "non-perception"?

Is it the cessation of the activity of the *guṇas*, or rather the non-arising of the *pradhāna-citta*—which has the nature of being seen, whose objects have been displayed, and which belongs to the Lord who is the seer? Or is it the absence of perception while its own object of sight still exists?
Or is it the purposefulness of the *guṇas*? Or is it ignorance (*avidyā*) that, having ceased along with its own mind, remains as the seed for the arising of that same mind?

Is it that when the formative forces of stability (*sthitisaṃskāra*) have perished, the formative forces of motion (*gatisaṃskāra*) become manifest? Regarding this, it has been said: "If the Pradhāna were to exist through stability alone, it would not be the Pradhāna because it would fail to produce transformations;
likewise, if it were to exist through motion alone, it would not be the Pradhāna because its transformations would be eternal. Its activity, however, consists of both."
It receives the designation "Pradhāna" (the Primary Cause) and not otherwise. Even when other causes are postulated, the same analysis applies.
Some maintain that the very power of vision is non-vision, based on the scriptural statement: "The activity of Pradhāna is for the purpose of manifesting its own Self."

The person (puruṣa), though capable of cognizing all objects of awakening prior to the onset [of manifestation], does not see; the object of sight (dṛśya), though capable of performing all functions, is then not seen. Some maintain that the non-perception of both is their inherent nature (dharma). In this regard, although this perception belongs to the very essence of the object of sight, it becomes a property of the object of sight in dependence upon the cognition of the person. Likewise, it is not an inherent property of the person.

Furthermore, non-perception appears as a property of the *puruṣa* itself, depending upon the conditions for perception. Some assert that non-perception is simply the absence of perception, which is to say, the absence of knowledge. These are the various alternatives found in the treatises. Among these, this multiplicity of alternatives concerns the common objects that arise when there is a conjunction of all *puruṣas* with the *guṇas*. (2.23)
But as for that conjunction of the conscious self with its own intellect, its cause is ignorance (avidyā). (YS 2.24)

The meaning is "the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of erroneous cognition. Furthermore, a *buddhi* permeated by the latent impressions of erroneous cognition does not reach the culmination of its task, which is the discernment of the *puruṣa*; it returns again as long as its office remains. But that [other *buddhi*] reaches the culmination of its task, which terminates in the discernment of the *puruṣa*; having fulfilled its office and with non-perception having ceased, it does not return again due to the absence of the cause of bondage.
In this regard, someone illustrates [the point] with the story of the eunuch: his foolish wife says to him, "Noble son, my sister has offspring; why is it that I do not?
He says to her, "I am dead; I shall produce offspring for you. Likewise, this existing knowledge does not bring about the cessation of the mind.

"What hope is there that it will cause destruction? To this, the teacher-like one (ācāryadeśīya) says: "Is it not the case that liberation is simply the cessation of the intellect (*buddhi*)? The cessation of the intellect occurs due to the absence of the cause, which is non-perception (*adarśana*). And that non-perception, which is the cause of bondage, ceases through perception (*darśana*). In that regard, liberation is indeed the cessation of the mind (*citta*)."
For what reason does this confusion of his intellect arise at such an inappropriate time?

(2.24) It has been stated that suffering is to be abandoned, as is its cause, which is called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) along with its instrumental conditions. What follows must now be explained: abandonment (*hāna*). From the absence of that [ignorance], there is the absence of conjunction; this is abandonment. For the seer who possesses this [abandonment], there is isolation (*kaivalya*). (YS 2.25)

The meaning is that due to the absence of that non-perception (*adarśana*), there is an absolute cessation of the bondage resulting from the absence of the conjunction between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*); this is "abandonment" (*hāna*). The meaning of "isolation" (*kaivalya*) for the seer—that is, the person—is the state of being unmixed, a non-conjunction with the *guṇas*.
When the cause of suffering ceases, the cessation of suffering is "abandonment."
Then it was said that the *puruṣa* is established in its own nature (YS 2.25). Now,
what is the means for attaining this relinquishment?—
undisturbed discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) is the means for relinquishment (YS 2.26).
The discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) is the cognition of the distinctness between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*. However, as long as false knowledge has not ceased, it fluctuates.

When false knowledge becomes like a burnt seed—its fruit-bearing capacity rendered barren—then, for the *sattva* whose impurity of afflictions has been shaken off, there arises a continuous flow of discriminative cognition as it abides in supreme clarity and in the highest state known as "mastery."

It becomes stainless. That discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), when undisturbed, is the means for the removal [of suffering]. Thereupon, false knowledge reaches the state of having its seed burnt, and thus there is no further production [of afflictions]; this is the path to liberation, the means for removal. 2.26 Its wisdom (*prajñā*) has seven stages of culmination. 2.27.

The word "of him" (*tasya*) is a reference back to the one in whom discriminative discernment (*viveka-khyāti*) has arisen. "Sevenfold" means that when the impurities of the veil of impurity have been removed and no further mental modifications arise, the wisdom of the discerning one is of exactly seven kinds, as follows: 1. "The object to be abandoned has been fully known; there is nothing further for it to be known. 2. "The causes of what is to be abandoned have been destroyed; there is nothing further for them to be destroyed. 3. "Abandonment has been realized through the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*). 4. "Discriminative discernment, which is the form of cultivation, has been practiced. [The remaining three types of wisdom are: 5. "The means of attainment have been practiced; there is nothing further for them to be practiced. 6. "The objects to be abandoned have been abandoned; there is nothing further for them to be abandoned. 7. "The goal has been attained; there is nothing further for it to be attained. Thus, for the discerning one, wisdom is sevenfold.

Regarding the "means of abandonment": this fourfold liberation belongs to wisdom (*prajñā*). However, the threefold liberation of the mind (*cittavimukti*) is the intellect (*buddhi*) whose functional authority has been exhausted.

Like stones fallen from the slope of a mountain peak, the *guṇas*—having no further station and being oriented toward dissolution into their own cause—set along with it. And for those that have dissolved, there is no further arising, due to the absence of any purpose.

Thus, in this state, the person (puruṣa) is beyond the connection with the qualities (guṇas), is stainless, consists solely of the light of its own nature, and is isolated (kevalī). One who contemplates this sevenfold wisdom of the ultimate stage is called "skilled" (kuśala). Even upon the re-absorption of the mind, he remains liberated and skilled precisely because he has transcended the qualities. 2.27

It has been established that discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) is the means for the removal [of suffering], and since this perfection does not occur without practice, the following is commenced:
"From the performance of the limbs of yoga, upon the destruction of impurity, there is the illumination of knowledge up to discriminative discernment" (YS 2.28).

The eight limbs of yoga are about to be described. From their practice comes the destruction—that is, the disappearance—of the fivefold error which consists of impurity. Upon that destruction, right knowledge becomes manifest. To the extent that the means are practiced, to that same extent impurity undergoes attenuation. And to the extent that it is diminished, [the manifestation of knowledge] follows the sequence of that diminution.

The radiance of knowledge also increases. Indeed, this increase reaches its culmination up until discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), meaning up until the direct realization of the true nature of the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*. The practice of the limbs of yoga is the cause of separation from impurity, just as an axe is for that which is to be cut. But it is the cause of attaining discriminative discernment, just as merit (*dharma*) is for happiness, and not otherwise.
Regarding the cause: how many such causes are there in the treatise? He says, "There are exactly nine. As it is said:
"Arising, persistence, manifestation, transformation, dependence, attainment, separation, alteration, and support—these are remembered as the ninefold cause."
In this context, the mind is the cause of the arising of consciousness;

the purpose of the person (puruṣārthatā) is the cause of the subsistence of the mind, just as food is for the body; and the cause of manifestation is, for example, light for form, while the cognition of form is [the cause] for that [light].

The cause of modification (*vikārakāraṇa*) for the mind is another object, just as fire is for that which is to be cooked. The cause of cognition (*pratyayakāraṇa*) is the knowledge of smoke for the knowledge of fire. The cause of attainment (*prāptikāraṇa*) is the practice of the limbs of yoga for discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*). The cause of separation (*viyogakāraṇa*) is that same [practice] for impurity. The cause of differentiation (*anyatvakāraṇa*) is, for example, the goldsmith for gold.

Likewise, for a single cognition of a woman, ignorance is the cause with respect to delusion, aversion with respect to suffering, passion with respect to pleasure, and knowledge of reality with respect to [the true nature of the object].

In the state of neutrality: the body is the cause of support for the senses, and they [the senses] are for its [the body's] sake. The great elements are the causes of support for bodies, and they are mutually so for one another;
likewise, those belonging to the animal, human, and divine realms are for one another’s sake.
Thus, there are nine causes. These are to be applied, as far as possible, to other categories of objects as well. This is the practice of the limbs of yoga.
However, causality is attained in only two ways. 2.28. In this regard, the limbs of yoga are determined:

restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi) are the eight limbs. 2.29.
We shall explain their performance and essential nature in due order. 2.29 Among these:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the *yamas*. 2.30.

Among these, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the absence of malice toward all living beings in every way and at all times. The subsequent restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) have that as their root; they are taught solely for the sake of its accomplishment and are adopted precisely to bring about its pure form.
And so it has been said: "Indeed, to the extent that this Brahmin desires to undertake many vows, to that same extent..."
Likewise, by turning away from the causes of violence committed through negligence, one practices that very non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) in its pure form.

Truth (*satya*) consists of speech and mind being in accordance with reality; that is, speech and mind correspond exactly to what has been seen and what has been inferred. Speech is uttered for the purpose of transferring one's own understanding to another; it should not be deceptive, erroneous, or barren of comprehension. This [truth] is for the benefit of all living beings.
It does not proceed for the purpose of harming living beings. And even if it were spoken in this way, if it were solely intent upon harming living beings, it would not be truth;

it would be nothing but evil. Through that semblance of merit, that counterfeit of merit, one would fall into grievous darkness. Therefore, having investigated, one should speak truth that is beneficial to all beings.
Theft (*steya*) is the appropriation of another’s property not in accordance with the scriptures;

its negation, moreover, is non-stealing (*asteya*), which consists of the absence of desire for such things. Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the restraint of the organ of generation when the senses are guarded. Non-possessiveness (*aparigraha*) is the refusal to accept objects due to perceiving the defects in their acquisition, protection, loss, attachment, and the harm they cause—these are the *yamas*. 2.30
But those [observances],
unrestricted by class, place, time, or circumstance, and universal in scope, constitute the Great Vow (mahāvrata).
In that regard, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) delimited by species is, for a fisherman, violence only toward fish and not toward others. That same [non-violence] delimited by place is:
"I shall not kill at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*). That same [non-violence] delimited by time is: "I shall not kill on the fourteenth day, nor on an auspicious day.

That same [non-violence], for one who has desisted from the three [delimitations], is delimited by occasion (*samaya*): "I shall not kill for the sake of gods or Brahmins, but otherwise [I may]. Just as...

For for Kṣatriyas, violence is restricted solely to battle and not elsewhere. Non-violence and the other virtues, when not limited by these [restrictions of] caste, place, time, or occasion, must be observed in every way. When they are practiced across all grounds, in all circumstances, and in every manner without any known deviation, they are called the "universal great vows" (sārvabhauma-mahāvrata). 2.31
Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances (niyamas).

In this context, purity (*śauca*) consists of external purification produced by earth, water, and so forth, as well as the consumption of pure substances; internal purity is the washing away of the impurities of the mind. Contentment (*saṃtoṣa*) is the lack of desire for more than the means at hand. Austerity (*tapas*) is the endurance of the pairs of opposites (*dvaṃdva*). These pairs are hunger and thirst, cold and heat, standing and sitting, and silence like a log (*kāṣṭhamauna*) and silence through gesture (*ākāramauna*). And their observances (*vrata*) are to be applied accordingly.
The *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, *sāṃtapana*, and other such penances; self-study (*svādhyāya*), which is the study of the scriptures on liberation or the recitation of the *praṇava*;
and devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*), which is the dedication of all actions to Him, the Supreme Teacher.
Whether lying on a bed, seated, or walking on a path, one who is composed and whose web of discursive thoughts has been destroyed [attains this].
Perceiving the destruction of the seed of saṃsāra, one who is ever-disciplined shall partake in the enjoyment of immortality.
Regarding that which was stated [in the previous sūtra]: "From these [arises] the realization of the inward-turned consciousness and also the absence of obstacles" (2.32), [it follows:

"When there is obstruction by *vitarkas* [unwholesome thoughts], one should cultivate the counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*) regarding these restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*). (YS 2.33)

When thoughts of violence and the like arise in this brahmin— such as, "I shall kill the wrongdoer," "I shall speak even falsehood," "I shall take his property," "I shall be unfaithful with his wife," and "I shall become the master of his possessions"— and he is thus afflicted by the intensely burning fever of thoughts inclined toward the wrong path;

One should cultivate their antidotes. One should reflect: "While being cooked in the terrible embers of *saṃsāra*, I have taken refuge in the yoga-dharma by granting fearlessness to all beings. Indeed, having abandoned those discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) and then taking them up again, I am equal to one who lives like a dog. Just as a dog licks what has been vomited, so too is one who takes up again what has been abandoned.
Thus it is; this [explanation] should also be applied to other sūtras. 2.34:

"For vitarkas such as injury (hiṃsā) and so forth—whether performed, caused to be performed, or approved; whether preceded by greed, anger, or delusion; whether mild, moderate, or intense—have suffering and ignorance as their endless fruits. This is the cultivation of the counter-measures (pratipakṣabhāvanā).

In this regard, violence (*hiṃsā*) is first of three kinds: committed, caused to be committed, or approved. Each of these is again threefold: by greed—for the sake of meat or skin; by anger—thinking "this person has done me harm"; or by delusion—thinking "there will be merit for me. Greed, anger, and delusion are further divided into three types: weak, medium, and intense. Thus, there are twenty-seven varieties of violence. [These are] weak, medium, and intense.

Again, it is threefold: weak-weak, medium-weak, and intense-weak; likewise, weak-medium, medium-medium, and intense-medium; likewise, weak-intense, medium-intense, and extreme-intense. Thus, violence consists of eighty-one varieties. Furthermore, through the distinctions of restriction, option, and combination, it becomes incalculable.
"Because the varieties of living beings are innumerable. This same principle should be applied to falsehood and the other [unwholesome thoughts] as well.

These aforementioned discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) have suffering and ignorance as their infinite fruits; this is the cultivation of the antidote (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*). That is, those for which suffering and ignorance are the infinite fruits—this is the cultivation of the antidote. And so, first of all, the one who harms [the victim]... [of the victim].
It impairs one’s vigor; consequently, it causes suffering through the falling of weapons and the like; thereafter, it even deprives one of life.

Because of this impairment of vigor, one’s conscious and unconscious implements become exhausted in their potency. Due to the arising of suffering, one experiences misery in the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and so forth.

Because he deprives others of life, even though he is at every moment on the verge of death himself and desires death, he somehow manages to breathe; for the ripening of suffering is necessarily to be experienced. And if, by some chance, his violence were accompanied by merit, then upon attaining happiness he would be short-lived. This should be applied accordingly to lying and the other [non-virtues] as well, according to what is possible.

In this way, by contemplating the undesirable ripening that follows upon these very discursive thoughts (*vitarka*), one should not direct the mind toward them. (2.34) When, through the cultivation of the counter-measures (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*), his discursive thoughts become subject to non-production, then the mastery resulting from that becomes an indicator of the yogi’s perfection (*siddhi*). For example: "When non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is firmly established, hostility ceases in his presence" (YS 2.35).
[This] occurs for all living beings. 2.36 When truth is established, there is the attainment of the fruits of action.
Thinking, "May he become righteous," he becomes righteous;
thinking, "May you attain heaven," he attains heaven; his word becomes unfailing. 2.36. When non-stealing is firmly established, all jewels present themselves. 2.37.
Jewels from all directions present themselves to him. 2.37.
When celibacy is firmly established, there is the attainment of vigor. 2.38.

By the attainment of which one enhances unimpeded qualities; and having attained it, one becomes capable of instilling knowledge in those to be trained. 2.38. Through the steadiness of non-possessiveness (*aparigraha*), there arises the thorough understanding of the nature of one's births. 2.39.

The inquiry into the nature of one's own self—such as "Who was I? How was I? What indeed is this? How indeed is this? Or who shall we become? Or how shall we become?"—arises in him regarding the past, the future, and the middle [present] states of existence. These are the perfections resulting from steadiness in *yamaniyama*. 2.39.
We shall explain the observances: from purity comes disgust for one's own body and non-association with others. (YS 2.40)
Beginning with purification out of disgust for his own limbs, the ascetic becomes one who perceives the defects of the body and one who is detached from the body.

Furthermore, avoiding contact with others and observing the true nature of the body, he desires even his own body to be abandoned; seeing no purity in the body despite washing it with earth, water, and so forth, how could he ever associate with the bodies of others, which are utterly impure? 2.40
Furthermore: "Purity of being, cheerfulness, one-pointedness, mastery over the senses, and fitness for the vision of the Self. (YS 2.41)
"they come to be"—this is the completion of the sentence. From purity comes purification of the *sattva*; from that, cheerfulness; from that, one-pointedness;
from that, mastery over the senses; and from that, the fitness of the *buddhi-sattva* for the perception of the Self. This is attained through the steadiness of purity. 2.41
From contentment comes the attainment of unsurpassed happiness.
And so it has been said:
"Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine pleasure there is—these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the bliss that comes from the exhaustion of craving. (2.42)
The perfection of the sense of touch results from the destruction of impurities through austerity.

As austerity is being performed, it destroys the impurity that constitutes an obscuration; from the removal of that obscuring impurity, there arises the perfection of the body, such as *aṇimā* and the rest. Likewise, there is the perfection of the senses, such as hearing and seeing at a distance.
From the study of sacred texts (*svādhyāya*), there comes communion with one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). (Yogasūtra 2.44)
The gods, seers, and perfected beings come into the sight of one who is devoted to the study of sacred texts (svādhyāya), and they assist him in his undertakings. 2.44.
Success in concentration (samādhi) arises from devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna). 2.45.

For one who has surrendered all states of being to the Lord, there is the perfection of *samādhi*, by which he knows everything desired—unerringly—in another place, another body, and another time. From that, his wisdom perceives things as they truly are.
2.45 The restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) have been described along with their perfections; we shall now speak of the postures (*āsana*) and so forth. Regarding this:
Posture is that which is stable and comfortable. (YS 2.46)

Namely: the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), the auspicious posture (*bhadrāsana*), the cross-legged posture (*svastika*), the staff-like posture (*daṇḍāsana*), the supported posture (*sopāśraya*), the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), the crane-sitting posture (*krauñcaniṣadana*), the elephant-sitting posture (*hastiniṣadana*), the camel-sitting posture (*uṣṭraniṣadana*), the balanced stance (*samasaṃsthāna*), the steady and comfortable posture (*sthirasukha*), and the posture as one pleases (*yathāsukha*)—these and others such as these. 2.46 [Posture is mastered] by relaxation of effort and by meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) on the infinite. YS 2.47.

The phrase "it comes to be" is the ellipsis [of the sentence]. Posture is perfected through the cessation of effort, by which the limbs do not tremble; or, the mind having attained absorption in the Infinite (ananta), it brings about the perfection of posture. 2.47. From that, there is no affliction by the pairs of opposites (dvandva). 2.48.
By mastery of the posture, one is not overcome by dualities such as cold and heat.
When that [posture] is present, the cessation of the flow of inhalation and exhalation is breath control (prāṇāyāma).
When mastery over posture has been attained, inhalation is the drawing in of external air,
exhalation is the expulsion of internal air,
and the cessation of the movement of both— the absence of both— is breath control (prāṇāyāma). 2.49
But that [breath], having its movement external, internal, or stationary, and being regulated by place, time, and number, becomes long and subtle. (YS 2.50)
Where there is an absence of movement preceded by exhalation, that is the external [breath]. Where there is an absence of movement preceded by inhalation, that is the internal [breath].

The third is the state of suspension (*stambha-vṛtti*), where both [inhalation and exhalation] cease simultaneously through a single effort; just as water placed on a heated stone undergoes contraction on all sides, so too do both movements cease at once. These are the three.

These too are "observed by way of place," meaning that their extent is determined as "this much is its range in space. They are "observed by way of time," meaning they are delimited by the determination of the number of moments (*kṣaṇa*). They are "observed by way of numbers": with this many inhalations and exhalations, there is the first upward movement (*udghāta*); likewise, when [the breath] is restrained, with this many [breaths] there is the second upward movement, and similarly the third. In this way, it is soft; in this way, middling; in this way, intense.

Thus has the [third] stage, characterized by counting, been described. This very [concentration], when practiced in this way until it becomes long and subtle, is the fourth [stage], which transcends external and internal objects. (YS 2.51)

[Prāṇāyāma] is that which is observed with regard to external objects and is restricted by place, time, and number; likewise, it is that which is observed with regard to internal objects and is restricted [by them]. In both cases, it is long and subtle. That which is preceded by this, wherein through mastery of the stages there is a gradual absence of movement in both [external and internal objects], is the fourth prāṇāyāma. The third, however, is the absence of movement not observed with regard to objects, which, having been undertaken once, is restricted by place, time, and number.

The first three are observed as long and subtle. But the fourth is the absence of movement, preceded by the simultaneous projection of both [inhalation and exhalation], resulting from the gradual mastery of the stages through the determination of the sphere of the breaths; this is the distinction of the fourth *prāṇāyāma*. (2.51) Thereafter, the veil over the light [of the mind] is destroyed. (2.52)

For this yogi who practices breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), that karma which obscures discriminative knowledge (*vivekajñāna*) is destroyed. Regarding that, they say: "Having veiled the luminous quality of *sattva* with a magical net consisting of great delusion (*mahāmoha*), it impels that very *sattva* toward what ought not to be done.
That karma which obscures the light and binds one to transmigratory existence becomes weakened for this practitioner at every moment through the practice of breath control.
And it is not exhausted. Thus it has been said: "There is no austerity superior to breath control; from it comes the purification of impurities and the radiance of knowledge. (2.52) Furthermore—
And there is fitness of the mind for the concentrations (dhāraṇās).
[This is achieved] precisely through the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), according to the statement: "Or [it is attained] by the expulsion and retention of the breath" (YS 2.53).
Now, what is withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*)?
Withdrawal is as it were the imitation by the senses of the nature of the mind when they are not in contact with their own objects. (YS 2.54)

In the absence of contact with their respective objects, the senses appear as if they conform to the very nature of the mind; thus, when the mind is restrained, the senses are restrained along with it, and they do not require any other means such as those used for the conquest of the other senses. Just as bees fly up after the king bee when he flies up, and settle down after him when he settles down, so too do the senses follow the mind.
When the mind is ceased, they are ceased; this is withdrawal (pratyāhāra). Thereafter follows the supreme mastery over the senses.

Some maintain that mastery over the senses (*indriyajaya*) consists in not being addicted to sound and the other objects of sense. Addiction (*vyasana*) is attachment; it casts one away from the highest good. The reasonable position is that there should be no opposition [to sense objects]. Others hold that it is the engagement with sound and so forth according to one’s own will. Some say that mastery over the senses is the cognition of sound and the rest that is devoid of pleasure and pain due to the absence of passion and hatred. [Others say it is] non-engagement [with objects] through one-pointedness of mind.

"So it is," said Jaigīṣavya. And therefore, this is the supreme mastery: that when the mind is restrained, the senses are also restrained, and they do not require any other effort-induced means as is the case with the conquest of the other senses. 2.55.
Thus ends the second chapter, the Sādhanapāda, in the illustrious Pātañjala Yogaśāstra, the exposition of Sāṃkhya, the commentary by the venerable Vyāsa. 2.2.55.
The five external means of accomplishment have been explained. Now, concentration (*dhāraṇā*) must be discussed: "Concentration is the binding of the mind to a place" (YS 3.1).

Dhāraṇā (concentration) is the binding of the mind by means of its mere activity upon locations such as the navel-center, the heart-lotus, the head, the light, the tip of the nose, the tip of the tongue, or upon external objects.
Therein, the one-pointed continuity of cognition is dhyāna (meditation). (YS 3.2)
In that state, the one-pointedness of the cognition whose object is the thing to be meditated upon—a continuous flow untouched by any other cognition—is *dhyāna* (meditative absorption).
3.2 That same [dhyāna], when appearing as the object alone and as if devoid of its own form, is *samādhi* (concentration). 3.3.

When meditation itself, through its nature as a mental state, becomes as if empty of the manifestation of the form of the object of meditation due to the absorption of the meditator's own being into the nature of that object, then it is called *samādhi*. 3.3.
*The three [dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi] together in one place constitute *saṃyama*.* (YS 3.4)

This triad of dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi, when unified, is saṃyama. These three means directed toward a single object are called saṃyama; this is the technical (tāntrikī) terminology for this triad. 3.4 From mastery over that [saṃyama], there is the light of wisdom (prajñā).

From the mastery of that restraint, there arises the light of the wisdom of samādhi; to the extent that the restraint becomes firmly established, to that same extent the wisdom of samādhi becomes confident. 3.5 Its application is to the stages [of meditative absorption]. YS 3.6.

The application of that *saṃyama* is to the stage immediately following the stage already mastered. For one who has not mastered a lower stage cannot attain *saṃyama* regarding the final stages by skipping over the immediately subsequent stage. And in the absence of that [mastery], how could there be for him the light of wisdom? Furthermore, for one who has mastered a higher stage through the grace of Īśvara, [there is no need for such application] regarding lower stages, such as the knowledge of others' minds and so forth.

Restraint (*saṃyama*) is appropriate. Why? Because its meaning is understood from another source alone. In the case of "this stage is immediately followed by that stage," yoga itself is the teacher. For it has been said: "Yoga is to be known through yoga;
yoga proceeds from yoga."
"But he who is heedful through yoga delights in yoga for a long time.
(3.6) The three [following] are internal compared to the previous ones. (3.7)

Thus, this triad of dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi is internal to cognitive (saṃprajñāta) samādhi, compared to the five previous means beginning with restraint (yama). But even that is external to seedless (nirbīja) samādhi. (YS 3.8)
Even that triad of means, though internal, becomes external to seedless yoga; why?
Because [the fruit] exists even in its absence.
Now, since the functioning of the *guṇas* is mobile, what kind of transformation of the mind (*citta-pariṇāma*) occurs at those moments of the restrained mind?

The transformation of cessation (nirodha-pariṇāma) is the sequence of moments of consciousness during cessation, characterized by the suppression of the latent impressions of emergence and the manifestation of the latent impressions of cessation.

The saṃskāras of emergence are mental factors (*cittadharma*); they do not consist of the causal conditions themselves, and thus they are not ceased when the conditions cease. The saṃskāras of cessation are also mental factors; through the suppression of the former and the manifestation of the latter, the saṃskāras of emergence diminish and the saṃskāras of cessation are accumulated. The mind follows the moment of cessation; this occurs for each single moment of the mind.

This alteration of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) is the transformation of cessation. At that time, the mind has only residual formative forces; this was explained in the context of the meditative absorption of cessation (YS 1.51). 3.10 Its flow becomes tranquil due to the [residual] formative forces.

The mind’s state of tranquil flow depends upon the proficiency gained through the practice of cessation and its formative impressions (*saṃskāra*). When those impressions weaken, the impression characterized by cessation is overcome by the impression whose nature is emergence (*vyutthāna*).
The transformation of the mind in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) consists in the waning of the capacity for all objects and the arising of one-pointedness. 3.11.

The state of being directed toward all objects (*sarvārthatā*) is a property of the mind (*cittadharma*); one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*) is also a property of the mind. The destruction of the state of being directed toward all objects means its disappearance; the emergence of one-pointedness means its manifestation. The mind is that which persists as the substrate (*dharmin*) for these two. Thus, this very mind, persisting through these two properties—which constitute its own essence—undergoes concentration (*samādhīyate*); this is the transformation of the mind into concentration (*samādhipariṇāma*). 3.11
Then again, when the subsided and the arisen have an identical object of cognition, that is the transformation of the mind into one-pointedness.
For one whose mind is concentrated, the preceding cognition is quiescent, and the succeeding one, similar to it, arises;

the mind of concentration follows both, and thus it remains just as it was, due to no lapse from concentration. This, indeed, is the transformation of the focusedness of the mind, which is the substratum. By this, the transformations of properties (*dharma*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and states (*avasthā*) in the elements and the sense organs are explained. (YS 3.13)

By means of this aforementioned transformation of the mind, which consists of the forms of dharma, characteristic, and state, it should be understood that the transformation of dharma, the transformation of characteristic, and the transformation of state are described with respect to the elements and the sense organs. Among these, the suppression of emergence and the manifestation of cessation constitute the transformation of dharma within the substrate (dharmī). Furthermore, the transformation of characteristic refers to cessation as having three characteristics [past, present, and future] across the three time periods.

It is thus: having first abandoned the future temporal state (*adhvan*), that which possesses the characteristic of the present has not transcended its essential nature (*dharmatva*) and has entered the present characteristic. It is therein that its manifestation occurs through its own form; this is its second temporal state.
And yet, it is not dissociated from the characteristics of the past and the future.

Likewise, emergence possesses three characteristics and is endowed with the three time-periods; having abandoned the present characteristic, it has not transcended its nature as a dharma and has entered the past characteristic. This is its third time-period. And yet, it is not devoid of the future and present characteristics. Thus, when emerging again, it abandons the future characteristic.

It has not transcended its essential nature (dharmatva) and has entered the characteristic of the present. That wherein it functions when its own form is manifested—this is its second path. And it is not devoid of the characteristics of the past and the future.
Thus again there is cessation, and thus again there is emergence.

Similarly, there is the transformation of state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*). In that regard, during the moments of cessation, the formative forces of cessation (*nirodha-saṃskāra*) become strong, while the formative forces of emergence (*vyutthāna-saṃskāra*) become weak. This is the transformation of state of phenomena (*dharma*). In this context, the substratum (*dharmin*) undergoes transformation through its properties (*dharma*); the properties belonging to the three times undergo transformation through their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); and the characteristics themselves undergo transformation through their states (*avasthā*).
Thus, due to the transformations of properties, states, and forms, the functioning of the *guṇas* does not remain devoid of activity even for a single moment.

And the functioning of the *guṇas* is mobile; indeed, it has been stated that the inherent nature of the *guṇas* is the cause of their activity. By this, one should understand that there is a threefold transformation among the elements (*bhūtas*) and the sense organs (*indriyas*), based on the distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*).

In ultimate reality, however, there is only one transformation (*pariṇāma*). For a property (*dharma*) is merely the essential nature of the substratum (*dharmin*); it is simply this modification of the substratum that is elaborated through the medium of its properties. In this regard, while a property remains within its substratum, there occurs a change in its state (*bhāvānyathātva*) across the time-periods (*adhvan*) of past, future, and present, but not a change in its substance (*dravyānyathātva*). This is just as when a golden vessel is broken and fashioned into something else.

"There is a change in state (*bhāvānyathātva*), not a change in the gold itself. Another says: "The substratum (*dharmin*) is not something additional to its properties (*dharmas*), because it does not transcend its prior reality. If this [substratum] were a persisting entity (*anvayin*), it would undergo transformation while remaining in a state of absolute immutability (*kauṭasthyena*), falling into the distinction between prior and posterior states; this would be a fault. Why? Because we do not admit an absolute [unchanging] position. Thus, these three worlds depart from their manifestation (*vyakteḥ*), because permanence is denied; yet even when they have departed, they still exist, because destruction is denied. This is due to their association with..."
And there is its subtlety, and from that subtlety there is non-perception.

Regarding the transformation of characteristics: a dharma existing in the time-periods (adhvan), when past, is conjoined with the characteristic of the past, [but] remains associated with the future and present [characteristics].

It is not dissociated from its two characteristics. Likewise, the future [dharma], while endowed with the characteristic of the future, is not dissociated from the two characteristics of the present and the past. Likewise, the present [dharma], while endowed with the characteristic of the present, is not dissociated from the two characteristics of the past and the future. This is just as when a man is attached to one woman, he does not thereby become detached from the others.

Regarding this transformation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapariṇāma*), opponents raise the objection that because everything would be associated with all characteristics, there would result a confusion of the time-periods (*adhvasaṃkara*). The rebuttal to this is as follows: the "dharma-nature" (*dharmatva*) of phenomena is not something to be established [by mere convention]. And since dharma-nature exists, a distinction between characteristics must also be stated; it is not the case that a phenomenon's dharma-nature exists only at the present moment. For if it were so, the mind would not have passion (*rāga*) as its dharma.
It might be argued that at the time of anger, attachment does not manifest.

Furthermore, it is impossible for the three characteristics to exist simultaneously in a single individual; rather, their occurrence would take place sequentially through the manifestation of their respective indicators. And it has been said that excellence in form and excellence in function are mutually exclusive.

The universals, however, function together with their specific intensities. Therefore, there is no confusion; just as when passion alone manifests in a certain instance, it does not mean that it is absent elsewhere at that time, but rather that it is merely possessed [there] by way of its universal, so too its existence is present there at that time—so it is with the characteristics. The substratum (dharmin) is not of the three times, but the dharmas are of the three times; they are characterized or uncharacterized therein, and those which are characterized therein [are the ones under discussion].
Those who attain that state are designated as being different due to their change of state, not due to a difference in substance.

Just as a single line is called "one hundred" when in the hundreds place, "ten" when in the tens place, and "one" when in the units place; and just as a woman, though being a single entity, is called a mother, a daughter, and a sister.

Regarding the transformation of state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*), some have raised the objection that it entails the flaw of immutability (*kauṭasthya*). How so? Because the time-periods (*adhvan*) are separated by their respective functions. When a property (*dharma*) does not perform its own function, it is future; when it performs it, it is present;

and when, having performed it, it has ceased, it is past. In this way, there would be immutability for the properties, the substratum (*dharmin*), the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and the states (*avasthā*).
The opponent states that this leads to a fault;

however, it is not a fault. Why? Because, even though the qualities (*guṇa*) are eternal, there is a variety of their mutual transformations (*vimarda*). Just as *saṃsthāna* (configuration) is a beginningless [actually, beginning-possessing] mere property (*dharmamātra*) of the qualities such as sound—which are both perishable and imperishable—so too the *liṅga* (the primal cause) is a mere property that possesses a beginning.
Regarding the notion of modification (*vikāra-saṃjñā*) in that [substance] due to the destruction and non-destruction of qualities such as *sattva* and the rest:

here is an illustration. The subject (*dharmin*), clay, while attaining another state from its previous state of being a lump, undergoes transformation (*pariṇamate*) in terms of its state (*dharmataḥ*) into the form of a jar. The form of the jar, having abandoned its future characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), enters into its present characteristic.

Thus it transforms according to its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). A jar, experiencing newness and antiquity at every moment, undergoes transformation of state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*). Since a state is another attribute (*dharma*) of the substrate (*dharmin*), and a state is also another characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the attribute, this is shown as a single transformation of substance (*dravya-pariṇāma*) through its various divisions. This should be applied similarly to other categories of things as well.

These transformations of properties (*dharma*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and states (*avasthā*) do not transcend the essential nature of the substrate (*dharmī*); thus, there is only one transformation that encompasses all these particularities. Now, what is this transformation? Transformation is the emergence of a new property upon the cessation of a previous property within a persisting substance. (3.13)
In this regard:
"The substratum (dharmin) conforms to attributes (dharmas) that are subsided, arisen, or unmanifest. (YS 3.14)

The property (*dharma*) is indeed the power (*śakti*) of the substratum (*dharmī*), as delimited by its capacity (*yogyatā*). And that [power], inferred from the diversity in the production of results, is observed to be both distinct and non-distinct in a single [substratum]. In that case, when the substratum exists while undergoing its own operation, it is distinguished from other properties—whether they be quiescent (*śānta*) or unmanifest (*avyapadeśya*). But when it is endowed with [the property] in a general sense, then...
Since [the distinctions] consist merely in the essential nature of the substratum (*dharmin*), what could be distinguished by what?
In this regard, those properties (*dharmas*) of the substratum are indeed "subsided" (*śānta*), "arisen" (*udita*), and "indescribable" (*avyapadeśya*).

Among these, the "subsided" are those which have ceased after performing their functions; the "arisen" are those currently engaged in their functions; and the "past" are those immediately following the present, which itself follows the future. For what purpose are they said to be immediately following the past?

Present [dharmas] do not exist [as such], because of the absence of priority and posteriority. Just as there is priority and posteriority between the future and the present, it is not so for the past. Therefore, the past has no immediate antecedent;
rather, it is the future itself that becomes the immediate antecedent of the present.

Now, as for those who maintain that [the categories] are indefinable because everything consists of the nature of everything: it has been stated that the transformational diversity of tastes and so forth in water and earth is observed in stationary beings; likewise, the qualities of stationary beings are found in mobile beings, and those of mobile beings in stationary ones.
Thus, through the non-interruption of their respective classes, everything consists of the nature of everything.

"Indeed, because of the restriction by place, time, form, and cause, there is no simultaneous manifestation of the selves. That which persists through these attributes (dharmas), whether manifested or unmanifested, having the nature of both the universal and the particular—that is the persisting substratum (dharmin). But for one for whom this is merely a collection of attributes without any persisting substrate, there is an absence of experience. Why?"

How can one [consciousness] be authorized as the experiencer of an action performed by another consciousness? Furthermore, there is an absence of memory for that [action], because one person does not remember what was seen by another. Moreover, due to the recognition of an object, a persisting substratum (*anvayī dharmī*) is established—that very substratum which, while undergoing a change in its properties (*dharmānyathātva*), is recognized; therefore, this is not merely a property (*dharma*) without a persisting substrate. 3.14
The difference in sequence is the cause for the difference in transformation.

Since it follows that there is only one transformation for a single substrate (*dharmī*), the difference in sequence (*kramānyatva*) serves as the reason for the difference in transformations. For example, the sequence is: clay-powder, clay-lump, clay-pot, clay-fragment, and clay-dust. That which is the immediately preceding state of a given property (*dharma*) is its sequence. "The lump ceases and the pot arises"—this is the sequence of the transformation of properties (*dharmapariṇāmakrama*).

The sequence of the transformation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapariṇāmakrama*) is as follows: for a jar, the transition from its future state to its present state is the sequence; likewise, for a lump of clay, the transition from its present state to its past state is the sequence. There is no sequence for that which is past. Why? Because immediate succession (*samanantaratva*) exists only when there is a relation of priority and posteriority, and such a relation does not exist for the past; therefore, sequence belongs only to two characteristics. Likewise is the sequence of the transformation of states (*avasthāpariṇāmakrama*).

Even in a brand-new jar, antiquity is observed at its edge. And that [antiquity], being manifested through a sequence following a succession of moments, attains its ultimate manifestation. This third transformation is distinguished by both the property (*dharma*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
These sequences acquire their own nature when there is a distinction between the property and the substratum (*dharmī*). Furthermore, even a property becomes a substratum.

"By way of the intrinsic nature of another property (*anyadharmasvarūpa*). However, when—in ultimate reality—there is a metaphorical attribution of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*) within the substratum (*dharmin*), and by means of that [property] the property itself is designated as being that very [substratum], then this sequence appears precisely as a unity. Within the mind (*citta*), properties are observed to be twofold: those that are perceived and those that are unperceived. Among these, those consisting of cognition (*pratyayātmaka*) are perceived, while those consisting of mere objects (*vastumātrātmaka*) are unperceived. And these latter ones are exactly seven, [to be known] through inference.
“Cessation, dharma, latent impressions (saṃskāra), transformation, vitality, activity, and power— these are the attributes of the mind, devoid of [objective] perception. (3.15) Therefore,
for the yogin who has acquired all the necessary means, the object of *saṃyama* is introduced for the sake of attaining the desired knowledge:
Through *saṃyama* on the three transformations, there arises knowledge of the past and the future.

Through *saṃyama* on the transformations of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the states (*avasthā*), and the forms (*pariṇāma*) [of things], knowledge of the past and future arises for yogins. The triad of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi* performed upon a single object is called *saṃyama*. By means of this, the threefold transformation being directly perceived brings about knowledge of the past and future regarding those objects. (3.16) Due to the mutual superimposition of word, object, and idea, there is a confusion among them; through *saṃyama* on their distinct separation, knowledge of the cries of all beings arises. (3.17)

In this regard, speech is meaningful only with respect to the phonemes (*varṇa*). The auditory organ, moreover, has as its object only the transformation of sound (*dhvani*). A word (*pada*), however, is to be apprehended by a cognition that synthesizes the sounds (*nādānusaṃhārabuddhi*). Since the phonemes cannot exist simultaneously and are therefore mutually independent in nature, they do not touch upon or bring about a word; thus, appearing and disappearing individually, each is said to have the nature of a non-word.

Furthermore, each individual phoneme (varṇa), being the essence of a word, is saturated with the capacity for all denotations; having attained a state of manifoldness as if through its opposition to other auxiliary phonemes, the preceding one is established in a specific state by the following one, and the following one by the preceding one.
Thus, many phonemes, following a sequence and delimited by the convention of meaning, are encompassed by the capacity for all denotations.
The phonemes *ga*, *au*, and the *visarjanīya* manifest an object possessing a dewlap and so forth.

Thus, that single mental reflection which arises from these [phonemes]—which are delimited by the convention regarding the object and whose sequential order of sounds has been withdrawn—is designated as the word (*pada*) that expresses the signified object. That single word is the object of a single cognition and is projected by a single effort.

The Buddhist [word-meaning], which is partless, non-sequential, and devoid of phonemes— being established by the operation of the cognition of the final phoneme— is understood by listeners through their worldly cognition, permeated by the beginningless latent impressions of linguistic usage, as something already established, by means of the very phonemes being uttered and heard with the desire to communicate it to another.

Based on that conventional understanding (*saṃketa-buddhi*), there is a distinction: the synthesis (*anusaṃhāra*) of this many [elements] of such a kind is the designator of a single object. The convention (*saṃketa*), however, consists in the mutual superimposition (*itaretarādhyāsa*) between the word and its object, having the nature of memory:
"This word is this object; this object is this word. Thus, it takes the form of mutual superimposition.
"Convention arises. Thus, these—word, object, and cognition—are intermingled through mutual superimposition:

"cow" is the word, "cow" is the object, and "cow" is the cognition. He who knows their distinction is all-knowing. Furthermore, in every word there is the power of a sentence; when "tree" is uttered, "exists" is understood, for the meaning of a word does not deviate from existence (*sattā*). Likewise, there is no action without an instrument.

And likewise, when "he cooks" (*pacati*) is uttered, there is an implication of all the factors of action (*kāraka*); the mention of the agent, instrument, and object—namely Caitra, fire, and rice—is a restatement for the sake of restriction. Furthermore, it is observed that the arrangement of words occurs within the meaning of a sentence, as in: "The Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) studies the meters (*chandas*)" or "He lives, he sustains the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). In that case, the word-meanings are manifested within the sentence; therefore, one should analyze and explain the sentence by first dividing it into its constituent words.

Whether it denotes an action (*kriyā*) or a factor of action (*kāraka*), otherwise—in cases such as *aśvaḥ* (horse) or *ajāpayaḥ* (goat-milk)—since these resemble nouns and verbs, how could they be analyzed as either an action or a factor of action when their specific nature is not yet determined? This is the distinction between those words, meanings, and cognitions. For example, in the expression *śvetate prāsādaḥ* ("the palace whitens"), the meaning is an action.

The word "white palace" has the sense of a *kāraka* (grammatical participant); its referent (*artha*) and its corresponding cognition (*pratyaya*) consist of both action and *kāraka*. Why? Because through the connection "this is that," the cognition and the convention (*saṃketa*) have a single form.
However, that which is the white object is the objective support (*ālambana*) for both the word and the cognition; for it [the object], by means of its own states...

When being modified, a sound is not accompanied by its conceptual object, nor is it accompanied by the cognition [of that object]. Thus, the sound is one thing, the conceptual object another, and the cognition yet another; they are not mutually concomitant. This is the distinction: the sound is of one nature, the referent of another, and the cognition of yet another. Through *saṃyama* on this specific distinction, the yogi attains knowledge of the cries of all living beings. 3.17
From the direct realization of the formative impressions (saṃskāra), knowledge of previous births arises. (YS 3.18)

Indeed, these *saṃskāras* are of two kinds: those whose nature is latent impressions (*vāsanā*) which are the causes of memory and afflictions; and those whose nature is merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) which are the causes of maturation (*vipāka*).

Formed by the intense volitions of a previous existence, they are mental factors (*cittadharma*) that are imperceptible, like the power of transformation, movement, cessation, or the property of life-force.
Mastery (*saṃyama*) over them is capable of bringing about the direct perception of those *saṃskāras*; and this cannot occur without the experience of their location, time, and causal conditions.

They possess direct realization [of these]. Thus, from the direct realization of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), knowledge of previous births arises for the yogin. Likewise, in other cases as well, through the direct realization of latent impressions, there occurs the perception of future births.
Regarding this, the following narrative is heard: [through] the direct realization of latent impressions, for the Blessed One Jaigīṣavya, in ten...

As he observed the sequence of births and transformations throughout the great cosmic cycles (*mahāsarga*), knowledge born of discernment (*vivekaja-jñāna*) arose within him. Then the Blessed One Āvaṭya, assuming a subtle body, said to him: "Because of your spiritual fitness (*bhavyatva*) throughout ten great cosmic cycles, your faculty of intelligence (*buddhi-sattva*) remained unsubdued; thus, as you beheld the suffering inherent in birth from the womb among hell-beings and animals, and were born again and again among gods and humans,"

"What was perceived as superior between pleasure and pain? Jaigīṣavya addressed the Blessed One Āvaṭya and said: "Throughout ten great cycles of creation, because of my spiritual fitness (*bhavyatva*), my faculty of discernment (*buddhi-sattva*) remained unsubdued; thus, having observed the suffering of existence in the realms of hell and animals, and being born again and again among gods and humans, whatever I experienced—all that [was inferior]."

"I perceive only suffering. The Blessed One Āvaṭya said: "This supreme mastery over the primary elements and this unsurpassed happiness of contentment that you possess—why is even this cast into the category of suffering? The Blessed Jaigīṣavya replied: "This unsurpassed happiness of contentment was spoken of only in comparison with the pleasure derived from sense objects; it is not so when compared with the bliss of liberation (*kaivalya*)."

It is indeed suffering. This property of the intellect-substance (*buddhisattva*) consists of the three *guṇas*, and since the cognition consisting of the three *guṇas* is placed within the category of what is to be abandoned, it is of the nature of suffering—the thread of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). However, because of the departure from the torment of the suffering of craving, this [state] is called happiness: serene, unimpeded, and favorable to all. 3.18
Through this practice, the supernormal knowledge of another's mind arises. (YS 3.19)
Through *saṃyama* on the mental modification (*pratyaya*), by means of the direct perception of that modification, there arises knowledge of another's mind (YS 3.19).
And that [knowledge] does not include the object [of the other's mind], because that object has not become an object for [the yogin’s own] cognition (YS 3.20).
One knows the passion, but one does not know that "it is passionate toward this particular object.

This is because the object of another's passion has not been made an object of the yogi’s mind; rather, it is merely the other person's state of passion that becomes the object of the yogi’s mind. 3.21.
Through *saṃyama* on the form of the body, when the power of its perceptibility is suppressed and there is no contact with the light of the eye, invisibility [is attained]. *Yoga Sūtra* 3.21.

By restraining the body from form, one obstructs that capacity of form which is to be grasped. When the capacity to be grasped is obstructed, there arises for the yogin the power of invisibility due to the non-connection with the light of the eye. By this, it should be understood that the invisibility of sound and the other [objects] is also described. 3.21
Karma is either with-impetus (sopakrama) or without-impetus (nirupakrama); through saṃyama upon it, there arises knowledge of the time of death, or [such knowledge comes] from portents (ariṣṭas).

Karma that ripens as lifespan is of two kinds: with an external cause (*sopakrama*) and without an external cause (*nirupakrama*). In this regard, just as a wet cloth spread out would dry in a very short time, so it is with that which has an external cause; and just as that same cloth, when gathered up, would take a long time to dry, so it is with that which lacks an external cause. Or, for example, just as a fire set to dry grass in a forest thicket by the wind on all sides...

When applied with effort (*sopakrama*), one may burn [fuel] in a very short time; likewise, when without effort (*nirupakrama*), that same fire, if applied to a heap of grass part by part in succession, would burn it only after a long time. In the same way, the life-determining (*āyuṣkara*) karma of a single birth is of two kinds: *sopakrama* and *nirupakrama*. Through *saṃyama* upon that, there arises knowledge of the end-point, that is, of death.

"Or from omens" (*ariṣṭebhyaḥ*): there are three kinds of omens—internal (*ādhyātmika*), external (*ādhibhautika*), and celestial (*ādhidaivika*). Among these, the internal is when one does not hear the sound within one's own body even with the ears covered, or does not see light even when the eyes are pressed shut. The external is when one sees the messengers of Yama, or suddenly sees deceased ancestors. The celestial is when one suddenly sees heaven or the *siddhas*. Or, conversely, when all things appear inverted; by this, one knows that the end is at hand.
Thus [ends the section on the powers]. 3.22.
The powers [arise] from friendliness and the other [virtues]. 3.23.

There are three meditations: loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and sympathetic joy (*muditā*). Among these, by cultivating loving-kindness toward beings who are happy, one attains the power of loving-kindness; by cultivating compassion toward those who are suffering, one attains the power of compassion; and by cultivating sympathetic joy toward those of virtuous conduct, one attains the power of sympathetic joy. The concentration that arises from such meditation is *saṃyama*. From that [arises]...

The powers arise with unfailing potency. However, toward those of evil character, there is only equanimity (*upekṣā*) and not cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Consequently, because there is no concentration (*samādhi*) in that [state], there is no power derived from equanimity, due to the absence of self-restraint (*saṃyama*) therein. 3.23.
Regarding the powers, these include the strength of an elephant and so forth. 3.24.

Through *saṃyama* on the strength of an elephant, one becomes possessed of the strength of an elephant; through *saṃyama* on the strength of Vainateya (Garuḍa), one becomes possessed of the strength of Vainateya; through *saṃyama* on the strength of the wind, one becomes possessed of the strength of the wind—and so forth. 3.24.
By directing the light of consciousness toward activity (*pravṛtti*), there arises knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, and the distant. YS 3.25.
The activity of the mind has been described as luminous; by fixing that light of the mind upon an object—whether subtle, concealed, or distant—the yogi perceives that object. 3.25.
Knowledge of the worlds [is attained] through *saṃyama* on the sun. YS 3.26.

The expansion of that [universe] consists of the seven worlds. Among them, from the Avīci hell up to the summit of Mount Meru is the world of the earth (bhūrloka). Beginning from the summit of Mount Meru up to the Pole Star (dhruva), the world of the intermediate space (antarikṣaloka) is variegated with planets, lunar mansions, and stars. Beyond that is the heavenly world (svarloka), the third world, which is fivefold and belongs to Mahendra. The fourth is the world of Prajāpati, Maharloka, which is threefold.
The Brahmā realm is as follows: Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka.
"The Brahmā world consists of three levels; beyond that is the great Prajāpati world;
and Māhendra is called Svar (heaven). In the sky are the stars, and on earth are living beings."
This is the summary verse.

Therein, situated one above the other, are the grounds of the six great hells—Mahākāla, Ambarīṣa, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Kālasūtra, and Andhatāmisra—which rest respectively upon solid water, fire, wind, space, and darkness. It is there that beings experience the sufferings acquired through their own karma.
