Living beings are born after having drawn forth a long life from misery. Beyond that are the seven netherworlds (pātāla) known as Mahātala, Rasātala, Atala, Sutala, Vitala, Talātala, and Pātāla. This earth is the eighth, the "Possessor of Wealth" (Vasumatī) consisting of seven continents, in the center of which stands Sumeru, the golden king of mountains. Its peaks are composed of silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, gold, and jewels; there, due to the reflection of the light of the lapis lazuli, [the mountain] appears dark like the petal of a blue lotus.
The southern part of the sky is dark blue, the eastern is white,
and the western is transparent.

The northern [region] has the appearance of the *kuraṇṭaka* flower. On its southern side stands the Jambū tree, from which this world is called Jambūdvīpa. Due to the movement of the sun, day and night proceed as if attached to it. To the north of that mountain are three peaks—Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgavān—each two thousand [yojanas] in length. Between them are three regions (*varṣa*), each nine thousand *yojanas* in extent: Ramaṇaka and Hiraṇmaya.

Regarding the Northern Kurus: to the south [of Meru] lie the Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himavat mountains, each two thousand *yojanas* in length. Between them are three regions, each nine thousand *yojanas* in extent: Harivarṣa, Kimpuruṣa, and Bhārata. To the east of Sumeru are the regions of Bhadrāśva, bounded by the Mālyavat mountain; to the west are Ketumāla, bounded by the Gandhamādana mountain. In the middle [is Jambudvīpa].
Varṣa is Ilāvṛta. This [region] extends for a hundred thousand *yojanas*, arranged in each direction from Sumeru at half that distance.

Indeed, this Jambūdvīpa, which measures one hundred thousand [yojanas], is surrounded by the salt ocean, which is twice its size and circular in shape. Beyond that, the continents of Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmala, Gomedha (Plakṣa), and Puṣkara are each double the size of the preceding one.
And the oceans are like heaps of mustard seeds, adorned with various mountain ornaments, containing the sweet waters of sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, whey, milk, and fresh water.
Encircled by the seven oceans, ring-shaped, and surrounded by the Lokāloka mountains, they are numbered at fifty koṭis of yojanas.
All this is arranged within the center of the well-established cosmic egg (aṇḍa), and that egg is but an atom of Pradhāna.
A part [of it] is like a firefly in the sky.

Therein, in Pātāla, in the ocean, and upon these mountains, dwell the hosts of gods, as well as asuras, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, kiṃpuruṣas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, apasmārakas, apsaras, brahmarākṣasas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and vināyakas. In all the continents dwell meritorious beings, both gods and humans.
Sumeru is the pleasure garden of the Thirty-three gods; there are the gardens known as Miśravana, Nandana, Caitraratha, and Sumānasa.

Sudharmā is the assembly hall of the gods, Sudarśana is the city, and Vaijayanta is the palace. The planets, lunar mansions, and stars, however, are bound to Dhruva; their movements are regulated by the constraints of the wind's dispersal, and they are situated one above the other over Sumeru.
They revolve in the heavens.

The six classes of gods residing in the realm of Mahendra are: the Tridaśas, the Agniṣvāttas, the Yāmyas, the Tuṣitas, the Aparinirmitavaśavartins, and the Parinirmitavaśavartins. All of them have their desires fulfilled, are endowed with sovereign powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest, and have a lifespan of one *kalpa*.
The *vṛndārakas* are enjoyers of sensual pleasures, possessing spontaneously generated bodies, and attended by Apsarases who are most excellent and agreeable.

In the great world of Prajāpati, there are five classes of gods: the Kumudas, the Ṛbhavas, the Pratardanas, the Añjanābhas, and the Pracitābhas. These have mastery over the gross elements, subsist on meditation, and have a lifespan of a thousand kalpas. In the first [world] of Brahmā...

In Janaloka, there are four classes of divine beings: the Brahmapurohitas, the Brahmakāyikas, the Brahmapārṣadyas, and the Amaras. They have mastery over the elements and the sense faculties, and their lifespans increase twofold at each successive level.
In the second world, Tapas, there are three classes of divine beings: the Ābhāsvaras, the Mahābhāsvaras, and the Satyamahābhāsvaras.

Thus it is said. These [beings] are masters of the elements, the senses, and primordial nature (*prakṛti*); their lifespans increase twofold at each successive level; they all subsist on meditative absorption (*dhyāna-āhāra*); their vital seed flows upwards (*ūrdhvaretas*);

their knowledge is unimpeded above and their range of knowledge is unobstructed regarding the lower realms. In the third world of Brahmā, the Satyaloka, there are four classes of deities who have not constructed physical abodes; they are self-supported, situated one above the other, masters of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), and endure for the duration of the creation.
Therein, the Acyutas possess the bliss of dhyāna accompanied by vitarka;
the Śuddhanivāsas possess the bliss of dhyāna accompanied by vicāra;
and the Satyābhās possess the bliss of dhyāna consisting of mere bliss.
Those who possess perception and the perceived, and who find happiness in the meditation on the mere "I-am-ness" (asmitāmātra), they too abide within the midst of the three worlds.

These seven worlds are all indeed the Brahma-worlds. However, those who have attained dissolution into the body-less state (videha) or into primordial nature (prakṛtilaya) reside in the state of liberation; therefore, they are not included among the worlds. This must be directly realized by the yogi by performing *saṃyama* upon the gateway of the sun.
Then one should likewise practice elsewhere until all this has been seen. 3.26. [By this,] knowledge of the arrangement of the stars in the moon [is attained]. YS 3.27.
Having practiced *saṃyama* on the moon, one should know the configuration of the stars. 3.27. Through [saṃyama] on the polar star (*dhruva*), there is knowledge of their motion. 3.28.

Then, having practiced restraint upon the pole star (dhruva), one should discern the movement of the stars; having practiced restraint upon the celestial chariots (vimāna) above, one should discern them. 3.28.
Knowledge of the body’s structure arises through restraint upon the navel-center (nābhicakra). 3.29.

By performing *saṃyama* on the navel-center (*nābhicakra*), one should know the bodily constitution (*kāyavyūha*). There are three humors (*doṣa*): wind, bile, and phlegm. There are seven constituent elements (*dhātu*): skin, blood, flesh, sinews, bone, marrow, and semen. Among these, each preceding one is external to the following; such is their arrangement. (3.29) By performing *saṃyama* on the hollow of the throat (*kaṇṭhakūpa*), there is the cessation of hunger and thirst. (3.30)

Below the tongue is a channel; below the channel is the throat; below that is a cavity. Through mastery over that, hunger and thirst do not afflict one. 3.30. Steadfastness [is attained] in the *kūrmanāḍī*. 3.31.
Below the navel, in the region of the heart, there is a channel shaped like a tortoise;
by practicing restraint upon it, one attains a steady state, just as a snake or a lizard does. 3.31.
By [practicing restraint] on the light in the head, there is the vision of the perfected ones (siddhas). 3.32.
By practicing *saṃyama* on the luminous light within the cavity of the skull, there is the vision of the perfected ones (*siddhas*) who move between heaven and earth;
or else, through intuitive insight (*prātibha*), everything [is known]. 3.33.

The intuitive knowledge (*prātibha*) called "the deliverer" (*tāraka*) is the precursor to the knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja*). It is like the radiance that precedes the rising of the sun. By means of it, the yogi knows everything upon the arising of intuitive knowledge. 3.33.
In the heart, there is the consciousness of the mind (*cittasaṃvit*). 3.34.
In this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-shaped dwelling; therein is consciousness. Through *saṃyama* upon that, there arises knowledge of the mind.

(3.34) Experience consists in the non-differentiation of the cognitions of the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, which are absolutely distinct. From *saṃyama* directed toward one's own nature—which is distinct from what is for the sake of another—there arises knowledge of the *puruṣa*. (3.35)

The *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhi-sattva*), whose nature is luminosity, having brought under control *rajas* and *tamas* through its connection with a corresponding *sattva*, undergoes transformation by means of the discernment that distinguishes between the *sattva* and the Puruṣa.

And distinct from that transforming *sattva* is the Puruṣa, who is absolutely dissimilar, pure, and of the nature of pure consciousness alone. Since their respective cognitions are not differentiated—despite the two being absolutely unmixed—experience belongs to the Puruṣa, because the object has been presented to him.
That object of experience (*dṛśya*), which is the condition for enjoyment, exists for the sake of another, namely the *sattva*.

However, there is another, distinct principle belonging to the person (*puruṣa*), whose nature is pure consciousness (*citimātra*). Through *saṃyama* directed toward that [consciousness], wisdom regarding the Person arises. And it is not by means of the cognition of the Person—which is essentially the *buddhi-sattva*—that the Person is seen; rather, it is the Person himself who sees.
One perceives that cognition as having its own self as its object; for it has been said: "By what, my dear, could one know the knower? (Brhadaranyaka Upanishad 4.5.15).
From that, intuitive knowledge, hearing, sensation, vision, tasting, and awareness arise. (Yoga Sūtra 3.36)

From *prātibha* [intuition] arises knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, the distant, the past, and the future. From *śrāvaṇa* [hearing] comes the hearing of divine sounds. From *vedana* [feeling] comes the attainment of divine touch. From *ādarśa* [vision] comes the perception of divine forms. From *āsvāda* [tasting] comes the perception of divine tastes. From *vārtā* [smell] comes the cognition of divine fragrances. These arise constantly. 3.36
These are obstacles to samādhi, but accomplishments upon emergence from it.

Those [powers] such as intuitive insight (*prātibha*), when arising for one whose mind is in a state of meditative absorption (*samāhita*), are obstacles (*upasarga*) because they are contrary to that vision; however, when arising for one whose mind has emerged from absorption (*vyutthita*), they are perfections (*siddhi*). 3.37.
Through the loosening of the cause of bondage and through the awareness of the movement of the mind, there occurs entry into another's body (*paraśarīrāveśa*). 3.38.

The meaning is that for the mind which has become dissolved and lacks a fixed support within the body, "bondage" is its fixation [on objects] due to the force of the latent impressions of karma (*karmāśaya*).

The loosening of that karma, which is the cause of bondage, occurs through the power of *samādhi*. Furthermore, the perception of the movement of the mind arises precisely from *samādhi*; and through the destruction of the bondage of karma and the perception of the movement of one's own mind, the yogi [attains liberation].
Having extracted the mind from one's own body, one places it into other bodies. Once the mind has been placed there, the sense organs follow it.
Just as bees fly up after the king bee when he flies up, and settle down after him when he settles down, so too do the sense organs conform to the mind during the entry into another body. 3.38
Through mastery over the udāna breath, there is non-attachment to water, mud, thorns, and the like, as well as the power of upward departure.
The activity of all the sense organs, characterized by the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, constitutes life.

Its fivefold function is as follows: *prāṇa* is the movement through the mouth and nose, operating from the heart upward; *samāna* is so called because it equalizes [the nutrients], operating from the navel downward; *apāna* is so called because it carries away [waste], operating from the soles of the feet upward; *udāna* is so called because it leads upward, operating from the head downward; and *vyāna* is pervasive throughout.

Regarding "vyāna": among these, prāṇa is the primary one. By mastering udāna, there is non-attachment to water, mud, thorns, and the like, and at the time of death, the soul's departure occurs; this [departure] is attained through mastery over it. 3.39. From the mastery of samāna, there is radiance. (YS 3.40)
Having performed the kindling of his vital energy (tejas) by conquering the breath (samāna), he causes it to blaze forth. 3.40.
Through saṃyama on the connection between the ear and space, divine hearing arises. 3.41.

Space is the support of all auditory organs and of all sounds, as it has been stated: "For all those whose hearing resides in the same location, there occurs the state of hearing from a single location. Furthermore, this non-obstruction of space has been declared. Likewise, because that which is formless is seen to be unobstructed, the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of space is also well-known. The auditory organ is inferred from the perception of sound; for between one who is deaf and one who is not, the former does not perceive sound while the latter does.
Therefore, for the yogi who has practiced *saṃyama* upon the connection between the ear and space, the divine ear—which has sound as its object—comes forth. 3.41.
Through *saṃyama* on the connection between the body and space, and by attaining the state of lightness like that of cotton, the power of moving through space arises. 3.42.

Where there is a body, there is space, because space provides room for the body; thus, there is a connection or attainment (*prāpti*) between them. Having practiced *saṃyama* upon that connection and mastered it, or having attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) in light things such as cotton down, down to the level of atoms, one whose connection has been mastered becomes light. And due to this lightness, one walks upon water with one's feet, and then, having moved over even a mere thread from a spinning wheel, [one moves through the air].

He dwells within the rays [of light], and from that, his movement through space becomes as he desires. 3.42. External, non-conceptualized functioning is the "great bodilessness" (mahāvideha); from that, there is the destruction of the veil of illumination. 3.43.

The acquisition of the mind's functioning outside the body is the concentration (dhāraṇā) called "bodiless" (videha). If that occurs merely through the external functioning of the mind while it remains established within the body, it is called "imagined" (kalpitā). However, the external functioning of the mind that exists only when it has actually left the body, independent of the body, is indeed "unimagined" (akalpitā). Therein, by means of the imagined [concentration], they accomplish the unimagined Great Bodiless [concentration].

Thus it is said. Through that *dhāraṇā* by which yogis enter the bodies of others, there occurs the destruction of the threefold veil—consisting of afflictions, actions, and their results—which obscures the luminous *buddhi-sattva* and is rooted in *rajas* and *tamas*. 3.44.
From *saṃyama* upon the gross, essential nature, subtle, sequential, and purposive aspects [of the elements], mastery over the elements (*bhūta-jaya*) is attained. YS 3.44.

In this context, the specific qualities such as sound and so forth, beginning with those belonging to earth, together with their attributes such as shape and so on, are designated by the term "gross";

this is the first form of the elements. The second form is their own commonality, which is expressed by the term "intrinsic nature" (*svarūpa*): solidity for earth, moisture for water, heat for fire, motility for air, and omnipresence for space; these constitute their essential natures.

Sound and the other [qualities] are the particulars (*viśeṣa*) of this generality (*sāmānya*). Thus it has been said: "For these things, which are endowed with a single genus, there is the exclusion of their mere properties.

Here, a substance (*dravya*) is a collection of generalities and particulars. For a collection resides in two [parts]: that in which the distinct parts have disappeared and are followed by [the whole], such as a body, a tree, a herd, or a forest;

and that in which the distinct parts are followed by [the whole] through being conveyed by a word, such as "both gods and humans," where one part of the collection is the gods and the second part is the humans, and the collection itself is denoted by those two.

And that [collection] is intended to be expressed as both distinct and non-distinct, as in "an orchard of mangoes" (*āmrāṇāṃ vanaṃ*) or "a community of Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇānāṃ saṃghaḥ*), which are termed "mango-orchard" (*āmravana*) and "Brahmin-community" (*brāhmaṇasaṃgha*).

Furthermore, it is of two kinds: that whose parts are established separately (*yutasiddhāvayava*) and that whose parts are not established separately (*ayutasiddhāvayava*). A collection whose parts are established separately is a "forest" (*vana*) or a "community" (*saṃgha*); one whose parts are not established separately is a "composite whole" (*saṃghāta*), such as a "body," a "tree," or an "atom. It is that which follows upon the distinctions among its parts that are not established separately.

Patañjali states that a collection is a substance (*dravya*); this has been described as their essential nature (*svarūpa*). Now, what is their subtle form? It is the *tanmātra*, the cause of the gross elements.

A single constituent part of that [whole] is the atom (*paramāṇu*), which consists of both the universal and the particular, and is followed by distinct parts that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*); such is the "collection" (*samudāya*). In this way, all the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) constitute this third [form]. Now, the fourth form of the gross elements (*bhūta*) consists of the *guṇas*, whose nature is manifestation, activity, and inertia, which follow the essential character of their effects, and are expressed by the term "concomitance" (*anvaya*). Then, their fifth form is "possessing purposefulness" (*arthavattva*).
The purpose of experience and liberation resides only in the *guṇas*;

the *guṇas* reside in the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), the primary elements (*bhūtas*), and their elemental derivatives (*bhautikas*). Thus, everything is meaningful. Now, through *saṃyama* upon these five elements, each possessing five forms, there arises for him the perception of the essential nature of each form and mastery over it. In that regard, there are five...

Having conquered the essential natures of the elements, one becomes a conqueror of the elements; through that conquest, the primary constituents of the elements become obedient to his will, like cows following their calves. From this, there arises the manifestation of the powers such as *aṇimā*, perfection of the body, and non-obstruction by the properties of those [elements]. (3.45)

In this regard, *aṇimā* is that one becomes minute; *laghimā* is that one becomes light; *mahimā* is that one becomes great. *Prāpti* is that one touches even the moon with the tip of a finger. *Prākāmya* is non-obstruction by desire: one emerges from and sinks into the earth as if in water.
*Vaśitva* is that one becomes the master over the elements and their derivatives, while others are not masters. *Īśitṛtva* is sovereignty over their origin, dissolution, and arrangement.

He exercises lordship. This consists in the power of determining objects according to one's will (*yatra-kāmāvasāyitva*), which is the state of having true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatā*), such that the fundamental natures of beings abide exactly as he intends. Even though he is capable of it, he does not effect a reversal of the nature of things; why? Because another previously established being who possesses the power of determining objects according to his will has already so ordained the dispositions of those beings through his resolve. These are the eight forms of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).

The perfection of the body (*kāyasaṃpad*)—which will be described later—and the non-obstruction by its constituent elements [means that] the earth, despite its solid form, does not obstruct the yogin’s bodily movements and so forth;

he even penetrates solid rock. Water, though moist, does not wet him; fire, though hot, does not burn him; wind, though moving, does not carry him away. Even in space, which is by nature unobstructive, his body becomes obstructed [to others], and he becomes invisible even to perfected beings (*siddhas*). (3.45)
Perfection of the body consists of beauty, grace, strength, and adamantine firmness.
He is beautiful to behold, radiant, possessed of extraordinary strength, and has a body with the adamantine compactness [of a diamond]. 3.46.
Through *saṃyama* upon the essential nature, the ego-sense (*asmitā*), the persistence, and the purposefulness of the organs, mastery over the senses is attained. 3.47.

The object of apprehension consists of sound and the other sense-objects, which possess the nature of both the universal and the particular; the functioning of the senses toward these objects is "apprehension. Nor does that [functioning] take the form of apprehending the universal alone; for how could that specific object, not yet discerned by the sense, be subsequently determined by the mind? Furthermore, the essential nature of the *buddhi-sattva*, which is luminous by nature, is a composite whole consisting of parts that are inseparably established as both universal and particular.

The substance is the sense organ. Of these, the third form is the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), characterized by the notion of "I-ness" (*asmitā*). The sense organs are the specific manifestations (*viśeṣa*) of that universal; the fourth form consists of the *guṇas*—which have the nature of determination and possess the qualities of illumination, activity, and inertia—of which the sense organs, together with the ego, are the transformation (*pariṇāma*). The fifth form is the state of being directed toward the purpose of the Spirit (*puruṣārthavattva*) which persists within the *guṇas*.

When there is restraint over these five forms of the senses, having achieved mastery in each respective instance, the yogin’s mastery of the senses arises from that mastery of the five forms. (3.47) Thereafter follows swiftness of mind, the state of being without organs, and mastery over primordial matter (pradhāna). (3.48)

The unsurpassed attainment of movement for the body is "swiftness like thought" (*manojava*). The state of "transformation of the instruments" (*vikaraṇabhāva*) is the attainment of the functioning of the sense organs even without a physical body, directed toward objects in any desired place or time. Mastery over *pradhāna* is the power over all primary causes and their modifications.
These three perfections are called the "Honey-like" (*madhupratīkā*), and they are attained through mastery over the five forms of the instruments. 3.48
For one who possesses only the discriminative discernment of the difference between the sattva and the puruṣa, there arises sovereignty over all states of being and omniscience. (YS 3.49)

For one whose *buddhi-sattva* has shaken off the impurities of *rajas* and *tamas*, who abides in supreme clarity and in the highest state known as "mastery," and who is established in the form of the mere discriminative discernment (*khyāti*) between *sattva* and the Puruṣa,

there arises the capacity to preside over all states of being. All the *guṇas*, which constitute both the means of cognition and the objects of cognition, present themselves to their master, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), as the totality of all that is perceivable.

This is the meaning. Omniscience is the knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*) which, by its very nature, arises simultaneously with respect to all attributes of the self (*sarvātman*), whether they exist as past (*śānta*), present (*udita*), or unmanifest (*avyapadeśya*).
This is the perfection known as "the sorrowless" (*viśokā*); having attained this, the yogi dwells as an omniscient master, his afflictions and bonds destroyed. 3.49
From detachment even toward that [subtle body], upon the destruction of the seeds of defects, there is isolation (kaivalya).
When he comes to this realization: "This dharma, which is the cause of discriminative discernment, exists for the sake of the destruction of the afflictions and karma of the *sattva*;

and the *sattva* has been placed on the side of what is to be abandoned; whereas the *puruṣa* is unchanging, pure, and other than the *sattva*," then, as he becomes detached from that [sattva], those seeds of affliction—which are like burnt rice seeds and incapable of germination—perish along with the mind (*manas*).

They proceed. When they have dissolved, the Puruṣa no longer experiences these three types of suffering. Thus, when there is a reabsorption of these guṇas—which had manifested in the mind in the form of the ripening of karma and afflictions and had fulfilled their purpose—there occurs for the Puruṣa an absolute separation from the guṇas, which is isolation (kaivalya). At that time, the power of consciousness (citiśakti), established in its own nature, is the Puruṣa alone. 3.50
Upon being invited by a celestial being, one should avoid attachment and pride, for otherwise there would be the risk of falling back into undesirable states. (YS 3.51)

There are indeed these four types of yogis: the beginner (*prāthamakalpika*), the one who has reached the stage of honey (*madhubhūmika*), the one whose light of wisdom is kindled (*prajñājyotis*), and the one who has transcended the need for cultivation (*atikrāntabhāvanīya*). Among them, the first is the practitioner in whom the light has merely begun to function; the second is one whose wisdom bears the truth (*ṛtaṃbharaprajña*); the third is the conqueror of the elements and the senses; and the fourth is one who, having performed the protective bonds regarding all things already cultivated and those yet to be cultivated, has completed the means of accomplishment.
But for one who has transcended that which is to be cultivated, the sole purpose is the relinquishment of the mind; his wisdom regarding the sevenfold ultimate stage is as follows.

There, when a Brahmin realizes the "Honeyed" stage (*madhumatī bhūmi*), the gods who dwell there, beholding the purity of his being, invite him to their abodes, saying: "O, sit here! Delight yourself here! This enjoyment is desirable."
"Delightful is this maiden; this elixir indeed wards off old age and death; this is celestial travel; these are wish-fulfilling trees;
holy is the Mandākinī; perfected are the great ṛṣis; favorable are the apsarases; divine are the ears and eyes;
and adamantine is the body—all this has been acquired by your long-lived self through your own virtues. May you enjoy this which is imperishable and ageless."
"The abode of the immortals is dear to the gods. Being addressed thus, one should contemplate the faults of attachment:

"By me, who am being cooked upon the terrible embers of saṃsāra and wandering in the darkness of birth and death, this lamp of yoga—which destroys the cataracts of the afflictions—has somehow been obtained; yet these winds of sense-objects, born of craving, are its adversaries."

"Having indeed attained this light, how could I—deceived by this mirage of sense-objects—once again offer myself as fuel to that very same blazing fire of *saṃsāra*? Farewell to you, sense-objects, which are like dreams and sought after only by wretched people! With his mind thus resolved, he should cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Without forming attachments, one should not even harbor pride, thinking, "In this way, I am to be entreated even by the gods. For through such pride, one will—due to a sense of self-satisfaction—fail to perceive oneself as being seized by Death by the hair;
and thus, heedlessness, which constantly watches for a vulnerability and must be guarded against with effort, having found an opening, will cause the afflictions to flourish.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence [of the practice being fruitless]. Thus, for one who does not engage in attachment or pride, the goal already cultivated will become firm, and the goal yet to be cultivated will manifest before him. 3.52.
Through *saṃyama* on moments (*kṣaṇa*) and their sequence (*tatkrama*), knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*) arises.

Just as the atom (*paramāṇu*) is the ultimate limit of the reduction of substance, so too the moment (*kṣaṇa*) is the ultimate limit of the reduction of time; or rather, that duration of time in which a moving atom leaves its former location and reaches a subsequent location is a moment. The continuity of their flow, however, is "succession" (*krama*). There is no real aggregation of moments and their succession; rather, it is an aggregation of the intellect (*buddhi*).

[These are] the moments, days, nights, and so forth. Indeed, this time, although devoid of objective reality (*vastuśūnya*), is a mental construction (*buddhinirmāṇa*) following upon verbal cognition; it appears as if it were the very nature of an object to those in the world whose vision is distracted by worldly activity. But the moment (*kṣaṇa*), on the other hand, is grounded in reality and depends upon succession; and succession consists in the immediate sequence of moments—this is what those who know time call "time."

Thus the yogins declare. Two moments do not exist simultaneously, nor is there a sequence between two co-existent [moments], because such is impossible. Sequence is that immediate succession of a subsequent moment relative to a preceding one; therefore, there is only the single present moment, and no prior or subsequent moments exist. Consequently, there is no collection (*samāhāra*) of them, as for those which have passed or are yet to come.
Those moments (kṣaṇa) are to be understood as being accompanied by transformation; thus, by means of that single moment, the entire world undergoes transformation.
Indeed, all these phenomena (dharmas) are mounted upon that moment. Through *saṃyama* upon both that moment and its sequence, those two become directly perceived.
And from that, knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*) manifests. 3.52
A specific distinction regarding its object is proposed:
because individuality is not delimited by genus, characteristic, or location, the cognition [of one] from [the other] arises from that [specific distinction]. (YS 3.53)

When two things are similar in their location and characteristics, the difference in genus (*jāti*) is the cause of their distinctness, as in "this is a cow" and "this is a mare. When they belong to the same genus and occupy the same location, the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is what effects their distinction, as in "the cow Kālākṣī" and "the cow Svastimatī. When there is similarity of both genus and characteristic between two *āmalaka* fruits, the difference in location is what effects their distinction, as in "this is the eastern one."

"This is the answer. However, when a previously situated *āmalaka* fruit is moved to a northern location by a cognizer who is distracted by something else, then—since they occupy the same space—the distinction that "this is the former" and "this is the latter" would be untenable. And since there must be knowledge of reality free from doubt, it was therefore stated: "From that, comprehension arises through knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*)."

How so? A location co-existent with a preceding *āmalaka* fruit is distinct from a location co-existent with a succeeding *āmalaka* fruit, and those two *āmalaka* fruits are distinct due to their experience of their own respective locations and moments. Furthermore, the experience of a different location and moment is the cause of their difference. By this example, [it is shown that] even for an atom whose location is identical in terms of genus and characteristic, there is a direct perception of the moment of the location co-existent with the preceding atom.

When the subsequent atom does not occupy that same location as the preceding one, the experience of that location by the subsequent atom is distinct due to the difference in their respective moments; thus, for both the Lord and the yogin, there arises the cognition of the difference between the two.
Others, however, explain that it is the ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣas*) which produce the cognition of difference; even in that case, there is a distinction characterized by location.

Difference in form, difference in obstruction, and difference in genus are the causes of otherness. However, since the difference between moments is accessible only to the intellect of a yogin, Vārṣagaṇya stated that because there is an absence of difference in form, obstruction, and genus, there is no fundamental separateness [of the elements]. 3.53.
The knowledge born of discrimination is "liberating," has "all things as its object," has "all modes of being as its object," and is "without succession. 3.54.

"Star-like" (*tāraka*) means that which arises from one's own intuition (*svapratibhottha*), not derived from instruction (*anaupadeśika*). "Having everything as its object" (*sarvaviṣaya*) means that there is nothing whatsoever that has not become an object for it. "Having all modes as its object" (*sarvathāviṣaya*) means that it knows everything—past, future, and present—in all its various aspects and in every way. "Simultaneous" (*akrama*) means that it grasps everything in every way as it ascends in a single moment. This is born of discrimination (*vivekaja*).
His knowledge is complete; its partial manifestation is the lamp of yoga, beginning from the stage known as Madhumatī until its final perfection.
(3.54) Whether one has attained the knowledge born of discrimination or not, when there is equality of purity between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, there is isolation (*kaivalya*). (3.55)

When the *buddhi-sattva*—having shaken off the impurities of *rajas* and *tamas*, having its sole purpose fulfilled by the realization of the distinctness of the *puruṣa*, and having the seeds of affliction burnt away—attains a state as if it were identical in purity with the *puruṣa*, then there is for the *puruṣa* an absence of even attributed experience; this is purity (*śuddhi*). In this state, isolation (*kaivalya*) occurs, whether for one who was a Lord or not, for one who possessed knowledge born of discrimination or another. For one whose seeds of affliction have been burnt, there is no further need for knowledge.
Someone might ask: "Has this sovereignty and knowledge born of samādhi been introduced merely as a means for the purification of the *sattva*?
But in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), it is through knowledge that non-seeing (*adarśana*) ceases; when that has ceased, the subsequent afflictions (*kleśa*) no longer exist.

Due to the absence of afflictions, there is an absence of the maturation of karma (*karmavipāka*). Furthermore, in this state, the *guṇas*, having fulfilled their office, do not present themselves again to the *puruṣa* as objects of vision."
When there is isolation (*kaivalya*) of the *tatpuruṣa*, then the *puruṣa* becomes pure and solitary, consisting solely of the light of its own essential nature. 3.55.
Thus ends the third chapter, the *Vibhūtipāda*, in the *Vyāsabhāṣya* on the *Yogaśāstra*, the exposition of Sāṃkhya by the venerable Patañjali. 3.3.
Perfections arise from birth, herbs, mantras, austerity, and meditative concentration.

Success through birth is that which is separated from the body, such as [attaining] medicinal herbs in the abodes of the Asuras or elixirs (*rasāyana*), and so forth. Through mantras, there is the attainment of traveling through the sky, the powers of *aṇimā* and the rest. Through austerity (*tapas*), there is success through mere will (*saṃkalpa-siddhi*), such as "having any form at will" or "going anywhere at will," and so forth; these successes born of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) have been explained. 4.1 In that regard, when the body and senses have undergone transformation into another species—
The transformation into another species occurs through the influx of primal nature (prakṛti).

The disappearance of the previous transformation and the emergence of the subsequent transformation occur through the entry of new constituent parts (*avayava*). Furthermore, the primary natures (*prakṛti*) of the body and the sense organs, depending upon causes such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth, sustain their respective modifications by means of replenishment. 4.3.
The efficient cause (*nimitta*) does not impel the primary natures; rather, it effects the removal of obstacles, like a farmer.
For merit (*dharma*) and so forth do not act as the motive force for the *prakṛtis*; a cause is not set in motion by its effect. How then [does it happen]?

"But from that [merit, etc. comes the breaking of the obstruction, like a farmer. Just as a farmer, wishing to flood another field from a field full of water, does not draw out the water with his hand—whether the [new field] be level, low, or lower—but rather breaks the barrier to the water.

When that [dam] is broken, the waters themselves flood another field; likewise, the *dharma* breaks the obstructive nature of the *prakṛtis*, and when it is broken, the *prakṛtis* themselves flood their respective transformations (*vikāra*). Or again, just as that very farmer is not able, in that same field, to force the watery or earthy juices into the roots of the grain, [so too is the case here].
Rather, it removes the mung beans, gavedhuka grass, śyāmāka millet, and so forth from that [soil]. Once these have been removed, the juices themselves naturally penetrate the roots of the grain;
likewise, dharma is merely the cause for the cessation of adharma, because purity and impurity are absolutely contradictory.

But it is not the case that *dharma* is the cause for the operation of *prakṛti*. In this regard, Nandīśvara and others are to be cited as examples; conversely, *adharma* also subverts *dharma*, and from that follows the transformation toward impurity (*aśuddhi*). In that case as well, Nahuṣa, Ajagara, and others are to be cited as examples. 4.3 But when a yogin creates many bodies, are they possessed of a single mind or multiple minds?
The minds of transformation arise from the mere sense of "I-am-ness."
Taking the mere sense of "I-am-ness" (*asmitā-mātra*) as the cause of the mind, one creates emanated minds;
therefore, they become possessed of mind. 4.4. Among the various activities, a single [root] mind is the motivator of many [emanated minds]. (YS 4.5)
How is it that the activity of many minds proceeds preceded by the intention of a single mind? [The yogin] creates a single directing mind for all minds;
from that, the differentiation of activity arises.
4.5 Among these, that which is born of meditation is without latent deposit (anāśaya).

The transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) is of five kinds; the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) arise from birth, herbs, mantras, austerity, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Among these, that very mind which is born of meditative absorption is "without latent disposition" (*anāśaya*); for it has no latent disposition (*āśaya*), meaning there is no activity of passion and so forth, and thus there is no connection with merit or demerit for the yogin because his afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted. However, for others, the latent disposition of karma (*karmāśaya*) does exist. 4.6
For this reason:
"The karma of the yogi is neither white nor black; for others, it is of three kinds. (YS 4.7)
This class of action is indeed fourfold: black, white-and-black, white, and neither-white-nor-black. Among these, the black belongs to the evil-minded;
the white-and-black is accomplished by external means. In that case, the accumulation of the store of karma occurs solely through the gate of harming or favoring others.
The white belongs to those devoted to austerity, self-study, and meditation; for that, being dependent on the mind alone, does not rely on external means.
It does not arise by causing pain to others. That which is neither white nor black belongs to renunciants who have exhausted their afflictions and are in their final bodies;
therein, it is "not white" because the yogi has renounced the fruits [of action], and it is "not black" because of non-attachment. But for other beings, there are only the three previous types. 4.7
Consequently, there is the manifestation only of those latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that are conducive to that specific fruition.
"From that" means from the threefold karma;

"only those conformable to its maturation" means that only those latent impressions (*vāsanā*) which are conformable to the specific maturation of whichever type of karma it may be—those impressions that lie dormant following the maturation of the karma—are manifested. For a celestial karma undergoing maturation is not the cause for the manifestation of latent impressions belonging to hell-beings, animals, or humans.

It is possible; however, only those latent dispositions (*vāsanā*) that are consistent with destiny are manifested for him. The same analysis applies to beings in the realms of hell-beings, animals, and humans.
4.8 Even for those [dispositions] separated by birth, place, and time, there is immediate succession because memory and latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) are of a single nature. 4.9.

The maturation of the experience of a cat, manifested by its own manifesting conditions, might be obstructed by a hundred births, or by distance, or by a hundred eons; yet, if it were to arise once again through those very same manifesting conditions, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) conditioned by that previously experienced maturation of the cat would immediately be manifested by taking that [impression] as its substrate. Why?
Since even for those [impressions] that are separated by time, a similar action serves as the manifesting cause and the efficient condition, there is indeed immediate succession. Furthermore,

because memory and the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) are of one and the same nature— just as the experiences were, so are the impressions— and since those impressions conform to the tendencies of karma (*karmavāsanā*), and just as the tendencies are, so is the memory, memory arises from impressions even when they are separated by birth, place, and time.
Furthermore, from memory come latent impressions (*saṃskāras*); thus, these memory-impressions manifest by virtue of gaining an active function through the storehouse of karma (*karmāśaya*).

Consequently, even for those [impressions] that are separated [in time], their continuity is established because the relationship between cause and effect is never severed. 4.9 And their beginninglessness follows from the eternity of the wish for life. (YS 4.10)

Because these latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are based on wishes that are eternal, they are beginningless. This wish for self-preservation—"May I not cease to exist; may I continue to be"—is observed in everyone, yet it is not inherent (*svābhāvika*). Why?

Because how could a newborn creature, who has never experienced the nature of death, have a fear of death caused by the recollection of the suffering associated with aversion? Furthermore, an inherent thing cannot be caused by an external condition.

It appropriates [objects]. Therefore, this mind, permeated by beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), acquires certain specific impressions through the power of objective signs (*nimitta*) and turns toward the experience of the person (*puruṣa*).

Others maintain that the mind—like a lamp in a jar or a palace—is subject to contraction and expansion, having a form and size exactly corresponding to the body; and thus, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) are logically established.

The Teacher [Vasubandhu] maintains that the very activity (*vṛtti*) of this all-pervading mind (*citta*) is what causes its contraction and expansion. And that [activity] depends upon causes such as merit (*dharma*).
Causes are of two kinds: external and internal. The external depends on means such as the body, consisting of praise, giving, salutation, and so forth;
the internal, consisting of faith and the like, depends solely upon the mind. Thus it has been said: "And these qualities of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth for those who meditate..."
Those meditative states (*vihāra*), being independent of external means, bring about the preeminent Dharma. Of these two, the mental is more powerful. How so?
By what could knowledge and dispassion be surpassed?
And who would venture to make the Daṇḍaka forest empty by means of physical action alone, apart from the power of the mind? Or one might drink up the ocean like Agastya.
(4.10) Because these [elements] are comprised of cause, fruit, support, and object, in their absence, those [elements] are absent. (4.11)
From dharma comes happiness, from adharma suffering; from happiness arises passion, from suffering aversion, and from that, effort.

By means of this [effort], moving through mind, speech, or body, one either benefits or harms another. Therefrom again arise dharma and adharma, happiness and suffering, and passion and aversion. Thus does this six-spoked wheel of saṃsāra revolve. Of this—

And ignorance (*avidyā*), which recurs at every moment, is the guide and the root of all afflictions (*kleśa*); this is the cause. As for the fruit, it is that which, depending upon [the cause], exists in the present state, such as the phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth;

for there is no production of what was previously non-existent. The mind (*manas*), however, is the basis for the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as long as its function (*adhikāra*) persists; for when the mind’s function has ceased, [the impressions do not remain].

Latent impressions (*vāsanā*) cannot persist without a support. Whatever object has become manifest and reveals a particular latent impression, that object serves as its objective support (*ālambana*). Thus, all latent impressions are subsumed by these four factors: cause, fruit, support, and objective support.
In the absence of these, there is also the absence of the latent impressions that depend upon them. (4.11)
Since there is no arising of the non-existent, nor the destruction of the existent, how can the latent impressions (*vāsanās*), which exist as substantial entities, ever cease? [The answer is:
"The past and the future exist in their own nature, because of the distinction between the temporal paths (*adhvan*) of phenomena (*dharma*). (YS 4.12)
The future is that whose manifestation is yet to be; the past is that whose manifestation has been experienced; and the present is that which is mounted upon its own activity.

These three objects are the knowable of cognition. If these did not exist by way of their own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), this cognition would not have arisen as being without an object. Therefore, the past and the future exist by way of their own nature. Furthermore, [this applies to] that which pertains to experience or that which pertains to liberation.

Furthermore, if the fruit of an action that is about to arise were non-existent (*nirupākhyam*), then the performance of wholesome deeds for the sake of that fruit and with that as its motive would be illogical. It is established that a cause is capable of bringing an existing fruit into the present, but not of producing something previously non-existent;
thus, a cause effects a specific benefit to the effect that already exists, rather than generating it anew.

The substratum (dharmin) possesses the nature of multiple attributes (dharmas), and its attributes are established according to the distinction of the time periods (adhvan). However, the past and the future do not exist substantially (dravyatas) in the same way that the present exists as a specific manifestation (vyaktiviśeṣāpanna). How then [do they exist]?
The future exists by its own inherent nature (svarūpa) as something yet to be manifested; and the past exists by its own inherent nature as something whose manifestation has already been experienced.
Thus, the manifestation of the intrinsic nature belongs only to the present path; it does not exist in the past and future paths.

Furthermore, at the time of one path, the other two paths necessarily remain associated with the substratum (*dharmin*); therefore, the three paths do not come into being after having previously been non-existent. 4.12
These manifest and subtle [objects] consist of the gunas.
Indeed, these phenomena (*dharma*) of the three times are manifest in nature when present, and subtle in nature when past or future; they consist of the six non-specific forms (*aviśeṣa*).
All this is merely a particular arrangement of the *guṇas*; thus, in the ultimate sense, they have the *guṇas* as their essence. And so says the instruction of the Śāstra:
"The supreme form of the *guṇas* does not come within the range of vision."
"But that which has come within the range of vision is as utterly void as a magical illusion.
(4.13) However, when it is asked how all the *guṇas* can be a single sound or a single sense organ—the reality of the object is due to the unity of its transformation. (YS 4.14)

The single transformation of the qualities (*guṇa*), which consist of the nature of manifestation, activity, and stability, and which are apprehending by nature, is the sense organ of hearing (*śrotra*) as an instrument;
the single transformation of those [qualities] which are apprehended by nature is sound (*śabda*) as an object, in the form of the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*).
And the single transformation of sound and the others—which are of the same class as material form—is the atom of earth (*pṛthivīparamāṇu*), which is a constituent part of that subtle element.

Furthermore, a single transformation— such as earth, a cow, a tree, or a mountain— and so forth, must be understood as a commonality arising from a single modification, based upon the presence of cohesion, heat, motility, and spatiality even among the other elements.
There is no object that does not accompany consciousness.

However, there are those who, following the line of reasoning that "there is indeed knowledge devoid of an object, as is imagined in dreams and the like," deny the intrinsic nature of reality, asserting that an entity is merely a mental construction comparable to the objects of a dream and does not exist from the perspective of ultimate truth. To them, [we reply]: how can this entity, which is present by its own majesty, be [denied] by that which is itself devoid of any means of valid cognition?
By the power of conceptual cognition, those who discard the true nature of an object and deny it would be persons whose words are not to be trusted. 4.14 Why is this unreasonable?
Because of the difference in minds despite the identity of the object, the paths of these two are distinct. (YS 4.15)
A single object that serves as the focal point for many minds is common [to all];
indeed, it is neither imagined by a single mind nor imagined by multiple minds, but rather is self-established. How so?

Because there is a difference in the minds despite the identity of the object: even when the object is identical, cognition of pleasure arises depending on merit (*dharma*), while [cognition of pain arises] depending on demerit (*adharma*).

From that very [object] arises the cognition of suffering, which depends on ignorance; from that very [object] arises the cognition of delusion, which depends on right vision; and from that very [object] arises the cognition of equanimity. By whom has this been imagined by means of a mind? Moreover, it is not logical that the coloring of one person's mind should occur through an object imagined by the mind of another. Therefore, the paths of the two cognitions of real entities—which are distinguished by the difference between the grasped and the grasper—are distinct.
There is not even a scent of confusion between these two.

Furthermore, according to the Sāṃkhya position, the objective entity consists of the three *guṇas* and is mobile; since the activity of the *guṇas* is thus, it becomes connected with the various minds depending upon causes such as merit (*dharma*). And for the cognition that arises in accordance with those causes, its cause exists in each respective form.
It exists. Some say: "The object is necessarily co-existent with cognition because it is something to be experienced, like pleasure and so forth.
By this line of reasoning, they refute its commonality [to multiple perceivers] and thereby deny the very nature of the thing in preceding and succeeding moments.
4.16 And an object is not dependent on a single mind; for if that [mind] were not a means of valid cognition at that time, what would the object be?
If an object were dependent solely upon a single moment of consciousness, then when that consciousness is distracted or ceased, the object would exist in its own form yet remain untouched by it;

being outside the range of any other [consciousness], it would lack any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*) and its intrinsic nature would be ungrasped. What, then, would that object be at such a time?
Furthermore, when it is again connected with consciousness, from what could it arise? Moreover, those parts of it that have not yet appeared—those too [would be unarisen].

If it were not so, then just as there is no "back," the "belly" would likewise not be perceived. Therefore, the object is independent and common to all persons, while the minds are independent and function according to each person; from the connection between these two arises perception, which is the experience of the Puruṣa. 4.16 Because the mind depends on being colored by that [object], the thing is known or unknown. YS 4.17.
Objects of sense, which are like magnets, attract and color the mind, which possesses properties similar to iron.
That object by which the mind is colored is known; any other than that remains unknown. Because an entity has the nature of being both known and unknown, the mind is subject to transformation. 4.17
But for one for whom that very mind is the object—his mental modifications are always known, because the Puruṣa, their master, is unchanging. (YS 4.18)

If the Puruṣa, like the mind, were subject to transformation, then the mental modifications directed toward him would be either known or unknown, just as objects such as sound and so forth are; however, the fact that the mind is always known by its master, the Puruṣa, leads one to infer his unchangeability. (4.18) It might be suspected that the mind itself will be both self-luminous and luminous with respect to objects, like fire—
That [cognition] does not have itself as its own manifestation, because it is an object of perception. (YS 4.19)
Just as the other sense organs and [their objects] such as sound are not self-illuminating because they are visible, so too the mind is to be understood.

Nor is fire a valid example here; for fire does not illuminate its own nature when it is unmanifest, and this illumination is observed only upon the conjunction of the illuminated object and the illuminator. Furthermore, there is no conjunction in that which consists of mere self-nature; moreover, [the mind] is self-illuminating.

The meaning of the word "mind" (*citta*) is that it is indeed ungraspable by anyone. This means, for example, that space is established in itself and not established in another. From the experience of the movement of their own intellects, the activity of sentient beings is observed—such as "I am angry," "I am afraid," "I have passion for that," or "I have anger toward that"—which arises from their own intellect.
"It is not logical [to claim] that there is no grasping.
4.20 And at one and the same time, there is no determination of both.
Furthermore, it is not logical for the determination of both its own nature and that of another to occur in a single moment;
for the proponent of momentariness maintains the position that whatever is the arising is itself the action, and that very thing is the agent.
(4.20) It might be thought: "The mind, which has ceased by its own inherent nature, is apprehended by another, immediately succeeding mind."
If one cognition were to be perceived by another cognition, there would be an infinite regress of cognitions and a confusion of memories. (YS 4.21)
Furthermore, if one consciousness were to be grasped by another consciousness, by what would the cognition of that cognition be grasped?
If it were grasped by yet another, and that by yet another, there would be an infinite regress (*atiprasaṅga*). Moreover, there would be a confusion of memories (*smṛti-saṃkara*);
for as many as are the experiences of cognitions of cognitions, so many memories would result. And from that confusion, there would follow the inability to determine a single memory.
Thus, by those nihilists who deny the person who experiences cognition in this way, everything has been thrown into confusion.

Yet, while they postulate the nature of the experiencer in some manner or another, they do not accord with reason. Some, however, even postulating a mere "being" (sattva), maintain that there exists a being who, having cast off these five aggregates, takes up others.

Having said this, they tremble once again from that very [state]. Likewise, having declared, "I shall lead the holy life in the presence of a teacher for the sake of great disenchantment with the aggregates, for dispassion, for non-arising, and for peace," they subsequently deny the very existence of the sentient being.
However, doctrines such as Sāṃkhya and Yoga, by their own terminology, accept the *puruṣa* alone as the master of the mind and the experiencer. 4.21
How so?—Because the consciousness, though itself non-transmigrating, undergoes the assumption of that [object's] form, there is the self-awareness of its own cognition. (YS 4.22)

For the power of the enjoyer is indeed unchanging and non-transmigrating; yet, as if transmigrated into the changing object, it follows its modifications. And because it merely conforms to that modification of the intellect (*buddhi*)—which has acquired the reflection of consciousness and whose true nature is thus apprehended—the activity of knowledge is described as being indistinguishable from the modification of the intellect. Thus it has been said:
“Neither the netherworld, nor a cleft in the mountains, nor darkness, nor the wombs of the oceans—
there is no cave wherein the eternal Brahman is deposited, which the seers perceive as the undifferentiated activity of the intellect.
(4.22) And for this reason, it is accepted as follows:
The mind, colored by both the seer and the seen, has all things as its object.
For the mind is colored by the object that is to be thought;
and since it itself is an object, it is connected with the subject—the Puruṣa—by means of its own function.
Thus, this very mind, colored by both the seer and the seen, appearing as both object and subject, assumes the nature of both the conscious and the unconscious.

Although its nature consists of objects, it is like something that does not consist of objects; although insentient, it is like something sentient; resembling a crystal gem, it is said to be "all-purposeful.

Because of this conformity with the mind (*cittasārūpya*), some are deluded and say that this [mind] alone is sentient. Others say: "All this is merely mind; indeed, this world consisting of cows, jars, and so forth, along with its causes, does not exist. They are to be pitied. Why?

For they hold that there is a seed of delusion: that the mind manifests in the appearance of all forms. In the context of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), the object to be known becomes a reflected image; because it serves as its objective support (*ālambana*), it is distinct [from the mind]. If that object were merely mind, how could the very nature of wisdom be apprehended by wisdom itself? Therefore, the object that has become a reflected image exists within wisdom.

"By which [consciousness] that person (puruṣa) is determined. Thus, due to the distinction in the nature of the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped, those who possess right vision distinguish these three according to their respective classes; by them, the Puruṣa is realized. 4.23 And for what reason? ————
Although that [mind] is variegated by innumerable latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it exists for the sake of another because it functions through collective action. (YS 4.24)

Thus, although this mind is variegated by innumerable latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it exists for the sake of another—that is, for the sake of the enjoyment and liberation of another—and not for its own sake, because it acts through aggregation, like a house. A mind that acts through aggregation cannot exist for its own sake; neither the mind of pleasure nor knowledge exists for the sake of itself or knowledge; both of these exist for the sake of another. And he who...

A person is truly possessed of purpose through the goals of experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*); he alone is the supreme [entity], not that which is merely a commonality (*sāmānyamātra*).

Whatever else the Nihilist (*vaināśika*) might cite as a mere commonality by way of its own nature, all of that must exist for the sake of another because it functions through combination (*saṃhatyakāritva*). But that supreme particular (*viśeṣa*), which is the Person (*puruṣa*), does not function through combination. 4.24
For one who perceives the distinction, there is the cessation of the cultivation of self-identity.

Just as the existence of a seed is inferred from the sprouting of a blade of grass during the rainy season, so too, when hair-standing-on-end and the shedding of tears are observed upon hearing the path to liberation, it is inferred that there exists within that person the seed of the vision of the particular, produced by karma conducive to liberation (*apavargabhāgīya-karma*). For such a person, a natural cultivation of the self (*ātmabhāvabhāvanā*) proceeds, the absence of which—

This has been said: apart from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), those who take pleasure in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) because of its defects and lack of taste for the final determination (*nirṇaya*) harbor such self-identity contemplations as: "Who was I? How was I? What indeed is this? How indeed is this?
Who shall we become? Or how shall we become? But that [contemplation] ceases for one who perceives the specific distinction; why is that?
"This is merely the manifold transformation of the mind;

the Puruṣa, however, when ignorance is absent, is pure and untouched by the attributes of the mind. Consequently, for the one who is skillful, the cultivation of the sense of self-identity ceases. (4.25) "At that time, the mind inclines toward discernment and leans toward isolation. (4.26)

At that time, his mind—which was previously inclined toward sense objects and submerged in ignorance—becomes otherwise: it becomes inclined toward isolation (kaivalya) and submerged in knowledge born of discrimination. 4.26.
In the intervals between those [moments of discriminative knowledge], other cognitions arise from latent impressions (saṃskāras). 4.27.

In the intervals of that mind—which is inclined toward the discernment of the conditions and flows solely with the cognition of the distinction between the sattva and the puruṣa—there arise other cognitions such as "I am," or "it is mine," or "I know," or "I do not know.
Why?
Because the seeds of previous latent impressions (saṃskāras) are being exhausted. 4.27
Furthermore, their [destruction] has been described as being like that of the afflictions.

Just as the afflictions (*kleśa*), having become burnt seeds, are no longer capable of sprouting, so too a prior latent impression (*pūrvasaṃskāra*) whose seed-nature has been burnt by the fire of knowledge does not give rise to conditions. However, the latent impressions of knowledge (*jñānasaṃskāra*) persist until the completion of the mind’s functional authority (*cittādhikārasamāpti*); thus, they are not taken into account here. 4.28

For one who is not even attached to discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), there arises, through the complete manifestation of discriminative discernment, the *dharmamegha* (cloud of dharma) samādhi.

When this brahmin is not indolent even regarding discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*) and thus desires nothing even from that, then for one who is detached even from that, there arises only discriminative discernment in every respect. Consequently, due to the exhaustion of the seeds of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), no further cognitions arise for him; at that time, his samādhi is called the "Cloud of Virtue" (*dharmamegha*). 4.29
From that follows the cessation of afflictions and karma. (YS 4.30)

From that attainment, the afflictions such as ignorance and the rest are scraped away along with their roots, and the accumulations of wholesome and unwholesome karma are destroyed along with their very foundations. When afflictions and karma cease, the wise person becomes liberated even while living. Why? Because error is the cause of existence. Indeed, no one whose error has been exhausted is ever seen to be born anywhere by anyone. 4.30
Then, because knowledge is infinite for one who is freed from all veils and impurities, the knowable is small. (YS 4.31)

For one who is liberated from all afflictive and karmic obscurations, there is infinity of knowledge (*jñāna*). The infinite essence of knowledge (*jñānasattva*), though overwhelmed and covered by obscuring darkness, becomes capable of apprehension only when it is set in motion and opened up in some particular place by passion (*rajas*). In that regard, when it becomes free from all stains of obscuration, then its infinity comes to be.
Because of the infinity of knowledge, the knowable becomes small, like a firefly in the sky. Regarding this, it has been said:
"A blind man pierced the jewel; one without fingers strung it; one without a neck put it on; one without a tongue praised it. (4.31)
Thereafter, for those whose purpose has been accomplished, there is the cessation of the sequence of the transformations of the guṇas.

With the arising of that Cloud of Dharma, the sequential process of the qualities (*guṇas*), having fulfilled their purpose, comes to an end. For those qualities, once experience and liberation have been accomplished and their sequence completed, they cannot remain for even a moment.

Now, what is this so-called "sequence"?—it is a sequence that is the counterpart of a moment (*kṣaṇa*) and is apprehended by its final limit within the process of transformation (*pariṇāma*). (YS 4.33)

Sequence is grasped by its final limit—that is, its conclusion—which consists of moments and immediate succession. For there is no state of antiquity in a cloth at its end that has not experienced a sequence of moments; and sequence is observed even in eternal things. This eternity is twofold: unchanging (kūṭastha) eternity and transforming (pariṇāmin) eternity. Of these, unchanging eternity belongs to the Puruṣa, while transforming eternity belongs to the Guṇas. That which does not lose its essential nature (*tattva*) while undergoing transformation is eternal; this applies to both cases.

And because it is not subject to destruction, its eternity is established. Among those, regarding the qualities of the *guṇas*—such as intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest—the sequence, which is discernible through their final limit of transformation, reaches a conclusion; however, regarding the eternal substrates, the *guṇas*, it does not reach a conclusion. Even in the case of the eternally immutable liberated *puruṣas*, who are established solely in their own essential nature, the existence of that essential nature is experienced only sequentially; thus, in that case as well, [the sequence does not terminate].
It is conceptually constructed by means of the pursuit of sound, based on the assumption of existence where no end can be found.

Now, regarding this saṃsāra, which proceeds through its qualities by way of staying and going, is there a sequential completion or not? This is not something to be stated categorically; for how is it that the question "Will everyone who is born die? is one to be answered with a definitive "Yes, sir"?

Now, regarding the question "Will everyone who dies be born again?", this is to be answered by way of distinction: one who has realized true knowledge (*pratyuditakhyāti*), whose craving is exhausted, and who is skillful will not be born; another, however, will be born. Likewise, when asked whether the human birth is superior or not superior, this question is to be answered by way of distinction: it is superior with respect to animals, but not superior with respect to gods and sages.

"No. However, this question—whether this *saṃsāra* is finite or infinite—is one that should not be answered directly. For there is a fault in restricting it to either alternative, since the completion of the sequence of *saṃsāra* occurs for the virtuous person (*kuśala*) and not for the other. Therefore, this question must indeed be explained [by distinguishing between the two cases].
When the sequence of the exercise of the *guṇas* reaches its conclusion, isolation (*kaivalya*) is attained; its essential nature is now determined:
Isolation is the cessation of the gunas when they are devoid of the purpose of the Purusha, or it is the power of consciousness established in its own nature. (YS 4.34)
Kaivalya (isolation) is the dissolution of the gunas—which consist of both cause and effect and have become void of the purpose of the Puruṣa once experience and liberation have been accomplished.

Furthermore, it is the Puruṣa’s establishment in its own nature due to the absence of connection with the sattva of the intellect; it is the state of the power of consciousness alone, remaining forever in that very same condition. 4.34
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Kaivalya-pāda, in the Yoga-śāstra known as the Sāṃkhya-pravacana, the commentary by Vyāsa on the illustrious Pātañjala [Yoga-sūtra].
